course.title: 用 AI，把日常事情做好
course.description: 带着真实公告、图片、指南和学习材料，完成清楚的表达、可信的整理、可执行的小计划与能分享的作品。
course.audience: 完全初学的成年人；不需要编程经验。可先用本课提供的真实公开材料完成判断与小作品。
objectives: 依据真实公告写出清楚且不夸大的短文。
整理有来源的信息，制作自己的学习卡和可交接的小计划。
完成一件能理解、能查证、能继续修改的小作品。

en.title: AI for Real Life
en.description: Use real announcements, images, guides and reading material to write clearly, organize trustworthy information, learn actively, plan a small task and finish a shareable piece.
en.audience: Adult beginners. No programming experience is required. Start with the real public material provided in the course.
objectives: Write a clear short message from a real announcement without overstating it.
Organize sourced information and make a learning card and a handover-ready small plan.
Finish a small piece that another person can understand, check and continue.

lessons.title: 同一份公告，不同读者先看什么？
lessons.content:
# 同一份公告，不同读者先看什么？

## 同一个图书节，朋友的问题却不同

[2024年美国国家图书节的公开页面](https://www.loc.gov/events/2024-national-book-festival)记录了活动地点、当天安排，以及部分节目直播、会后提供全部节目录像的说明。

你要根据这份历史材料写一段短导览。一位读者关心当年现场如何参加；另一位没能到场，想了解远程观看的办法。你只准备给每人两句话。

## 先猜一下

两段话的篇幅相同，你会怎样决定各自先放哪些信息？

先写下你的判断，再往下看答案。

## 答案

先看读者要做什么，再选择能帮助那个动作的信息。现场安排与远程观看都来自同一页面，但不必在两段导览里占相同位置。

## 先把读者的问题写成一句话

在原文旁写下：“这位读者想查当年的现场安排。”或“这位读者想知道怎样查看节目。”然后只挑回答这个问题的内容。

可以向助手这样交代：“根据这份2024年记录，给未能到场的人写两句资料导览，说明远程观看的范围，并保留原始入口。”先有用途，再调整语气。

:::detail[为什么不把所有信息都给每个读者？]
两句话的空间有限。你把现场地址、开门时间、作者名单与录像安排全部塞进去，读者反而可能找不到自己需要的动作。这不是说其他事实没有价值，而是这份短导览先解决一个问题。完整页面可以承担其余信息。你可以先在纸上写下读者的问题，再逐项问：这个细节能否帮他回答这个问题？如果没有，就不必抢占开头的位置。[W3C的写作提示](https://www.w3.org/WAI/tips/writing/)强调清楚的内容组织与有意义的链接，在这里可以落实为一段有明确方向的文字。
:::

为两位读者选择短导览的重点。两种重点都有用，取决于当前的问题。

::play{#who-will-read-this-weigh}

## 什么时候该反过来

要做供不同人查阅的完整资料页时，可以按现场、远程等主题分区，让读者自己进入对应部分。短消息与公共资料页，不需要采用同一种信息排序。

:::detail[读者没有说自己要什么，先猜一个身份可以吗？]
可以先问一个会改变成品的问题，例如“你要查现场安排，还是远程节目资料？”这比要求读者填写许多个人信息更直接。若暂时无法追问，就把自己的暂定范围说清楚，例如“下面先整理远程观看说明，现场安排见原页面”。不要偷偷替读者决定他需要什么，再把没有用上的信息都说成多余。你在做的是一个有范围的编辑选择，而不是判断所有人应该怎样阅读。
:::

:::detail[两个读者都需要年份，为什么还要分别写？]
不同读者可以共享某些必要信息。2024年的历史身份帮助两个人都知道材料属于哪一次活动；接下来才根据各自的任务选择现场时间或观看方式。面向读者并不是每个字都要不同，而是知道哪些相同信息仍然重要，哪些应该调整位置。先保留共同的事实底座，再改变重点，就不会为了表现差异，把同一活动写成两件不同的事。完成两段文字后，用原页面分别核对一次。
:::

## 自检

现在读者只想查某位作者的节目记录。你会把哪一种信息提到前面，又把哪些活动背景留给原始页面？

## 一句话

**同一份真实材料，先回答这个读者要解决的问题。**

en.title: The Same Announcement: What Do Different Readers Look for First?
en.content:
# The Same Announcement: What Do Different Readers Look for First?

## The Same Book Festival, but Friends Have Different Questions

The [public page for the 2024 National Book Festival](https://www.loc.gov/events/2024-national-book-festival) records the event location, the schedule for the day, and notes that some sessions would be livestreamed while recordings of all sessions would be provided after the festival.

You need to write a short guide based on this historical material. One reader wants to know how to attend in person back then; another could not attend and wants to learn about ways to watch remotely. You plan to give each person only two sentences.

## Predict first
With both guides being the same length, how would you decide what information to put first in each?

Write down your decision first, then read on for the answer.

## Answer
First look at what the reader needs to do, then choose the information that helps with that action. The in-person schedule and the remote viewing options both come from the same page, but they do not need to take up the same position in both guides.

## First put the reader's question into one sentence

Next to the original text, write down: "This reader wants to look up the in-person schedule from that year," or "This reader wants to know how to view the sessions." Then select only the content that answers that question.

You can give instructions to an assistant like this: "Based on this 2024 record, write a two-sentence guide for people who could not attend, explaining the scope of remote viewing and keeping the original link." Establish the purpose first, then adjust the tone.

:::detail[Why not give all the information to every reader?]
Space is limited in two sentences. If you cram in the venue address, opening times, author list, and recording schedule all at once, readers may struggle to find the action they need. This does not mean other facts have no value; rather, this short guide solves one problem first. The full page can carry the remaining information. You can write the reader's question on paper first, then ask for each detail: does this help answer their question? If not, it does not need to take up space at the beginning. The [W3C writing tips](https://www.w3.org/WAI/tips/writing/) emphasize clear content organization and meaningful links, which here can translate into a passage with a clear sense of direction.
:::

Choose the focus of the short guide for each of the two readers. Both points of focus are useful, depending on the question at hand.

::play{#who-will-read-this-weigh}

## When to choose the other way

When creating a full reference page for different people to consult, you can organize it into sections by topic—such as in-person attendance or remote access—so readers can navigate to the section they need. Short messages and public reference pages do not need to use the same ordering of information.

:::detail[If a reader hasn't said what they want, is it okay to guess an identity first?]
You can start by asking a question that will change the final product, such as "Are you looking for in-person details or remote session materials?" This is more direct than asking the reader to fill in a lot of personal information. If you cannot follow up right away, state your tentative scope clearly—for example, "The following summarizes remote viewing instructions; see the original page for in-person arrangements." Don't quietly decide for the reader what they need and then dismiss unused details as superfluous. You are making a scoped editorial choice, not deciding how everyone ought to read.
:::

:::detail[Both readers need the year, so why write for them separately?]
Different readers can share certain essential information. The 2024 date helps both people know which specific event the material belongs to; only then do they select in-person times or viewing methods based on their respective tasks. Writing for different readers does not mean every word has to be different—it means knowing which shared facts remain important and which need to be repositioned. By keeping a shared factual foundation before shifting the emphasis, you avoid turning the same event into two completely different things just to show contrast. After finishing both passages, check each one against the original page.
:::

## Check yourself
Now suppose a reader only wants to look up a specific author's session record. Which information would you move to the front, and which event background details would you leave to the original page?

## In one sentence
**From the same factual material, answer the question this reader needs to solve first.**

lessons.title: 缩成两句话，什么绝不能被挤掉？
lessons.content:
# 缩成两句话，什么绝不能被挤掉？

## 8:30与9:00，哪一个可以省略？

[2024年图书节页面](https://www.loc.gov/events/2024-national-book-festival)说明：活动当天9:00开始，8:30开门。你正在编辑当年现场安排的历史小卡，想把这段话缩短。

一份待改稿写成：“活动8:30开始。”它更短了，两个时间也只剩一个。

## 先猜一下

这份缩写改变了什么，你会怎样在变短时保留真正需要的信息？

先写下你的判断，再往下看答案。

## 答案

它把开门时间改成了活动开始时间。可以缩短表达，却不能把两个不同动作合并成一个错误的安排。

## 先圈出不能改错的事实，再动字数

先给时间配上动作：“8:30开门；9:00开始。”再决定卡片是否需要两项都写。只介绍节目开始，可以只保留9:00；介绍现场入场安排，则应让两项的区别仍然清楚。

现在亲自改写一次：用一句短话保留这两个动作，再与原页面对应位置比对。不要只数减少了几个字。

:::detail[删掉一项真实信息，也一定是不准确吗？]
不一定。短文必然要选择内容，关键在于删掉后剩下的话是否仍然真实，并且够当前读者使用。例如“活动9:00开始”没有说明开门时间，但并没有把开始时间改错；若读者要研究当年的进场安排，它可能不够完整，需要另补8:30开门。要分开判断准确与充分：一句话可以没说错，却仍没回答读者的问题。先核对留下的意思，再检查是否漏掉影响读者动作的条件。
:::

:::detail[怎样向助手说明哪些地方不能缩掉？]
把条件写成可以逐项检查的要求：“请缩成一句，但保持开门与开始是两个不同动作，不改变对应时间。”这比“别丢重点”更具体，因为重点已经有名字。拿到改稿后，仍要自己对照：8:30旁边是不是开门，9:00旁边是不是开始。助手答应保留，不代表已经保留。你可以把改前与改后并排放着，只核对这一项，再处理其他需要缩短的部分。
:::

:::detail[一段文字确实放不下全部必要内容，怎么办？]
不要用错误合并来节省空间。可以保留当前读者最需要的一句，再用有意义的链接指向完整安排，例如“查看2024年活动说明”。[W3C写作提示](https://www.w3.org/WAI/tips/writing/)中的简洁与清楚，不等于让所有条件消失。也可以换成两行、短清单或稍大的卡片，只要仍适合使用场景。版面限制与事实准确发生冲突时，先调整版面或信息分层，而不是悄悄改写原始事实。
:::

这些句子是对真实公告的教学改写，不是已经发出的通知。判断留下的意思是否仍与原文一致。

::play{#keep-the-facts-while-shortening-sort}

## 自检

原页面只说部分节目直播，你把说明压成“节目直播”。这句话可能让读者多相信什么？怎样改短又不扩大范围？

## 一句话

**缩写可以少说一些，不可以把留下来的事实换成别的意思。**

en.title: When Shortening to Two Sentences, What Must Never Be Squeezed Out?
en.content:
# When Shortening to Two Sentences, What Must Never Be Squeezed Out?

## 8:30 and 9:00: Which One Can Be Omitted?

The [2024 National Book Festival page](https://www.loc.gov/events/2024-national-book-festival) states: on the day of the event, the event starts at 9:00 and doors open at 8:30. You are editing a historical note card about that year's on-site arrangements and want to shorten this passage.

One draft to be revised reads: "The event starts at 8:30." It is shorter, and only one of the two times remains.

## Predict first
What did this shortening change, and how would you preserve the information that is truly needed while making it shorter?

Write down your judgment first before reading the answer below.

## Answer
It turned the door-opening time into the event's start time. You can shorten phrasing, but you cannot merge two different actions into an incorrect arrangement.

## Circle the Facts That Must Not Be Changed Before Adjusting the Word Count

First pair each time with its action: "Doors open at 8:30; starts at 9:00." Then decide whether the card needs both items. If you are only introducing the start of the program, you can keep only 9:00; if you are introducing the on-site admission arrangements, you should keep the distinction between the two items clear.

Now rewrite it yourself once: use a single short sentence to preserve both actions, and then compare it with the corresponding spot on the original page. Do not just count how many words were cut.

:::detail[Does deleting a piece of true information necessarily mean it is inaccurate?]
Not necessarily. A short text inevitably involves choosing what to include; the key is whether what remains after deletion is still true and adequate for the current reader. For example, "The event starts at 9:00" does not state the door-opening time, but it does not get the start time wrong; if a reader wants to research that year's admission arrangements, it may not be complete enough and would require adding that doors open at 8:30. You need to judge accuracy and adequacy separately: a sentence can contain no errors yet still fail to answer the reader's question. First verify what the remaining meaning says, then check whether you left out conditions that affect the reader's actions.
:::

:::detail[How do you explain to an assistant what cannot be cut?]
Write conditions as requirements that can be checked item by item: "Please shorten this to one sentence, but keep opening doors and starting as two distinct actions, without changing their corresponding times." This is more specific than "don't drop the key points," because the key points have names. After getting the revised draft, you still need to verify it yourself: is opening doors next to 8:30, and is starting next to 9:00? An assistant agreeing to keep something does not mean it has been kept. You can place the version before revision side by side with the one after, verify just this item, and then address the other parts that need shortening.
:::

:::detail[What should you do if a piece of text genuinely cannot fit all the necessary content?]
Do not save space through incorrect merging. You can keep the single sentence your current readers need most, and use a meaningful link pointing to the full schedule, such as "View the 2024 event details." Conciseness and clarity in the [W3C writing tips](https://www.w3.org/WAI/tips/writing/) do not mean making all conditions disappear. You can also switch to two lines, a short list, or a slightly larger card, as long as it still fits the use case. When layout limits conflict with factual accuracy, adjust the layout or information hierarchy first, rather than quietly rewriting the original facts.
:::

These sentences are pedagogical rewrites of a real announcement, not notices that were actually sent. Judge whether the remaining meaning is still consistent with the original.

::play{#keep-the-facts-while-shortening-sort}

## Check yourself
The original page only said some programs would be live-streamed, but you compressed the description into "programs live-streamed." What extra assumptions might this sentence lead readers to believe? How can you shorten it without widening the scope?

## In one sentence
**Shortening can say less, but it must not change the remaining facts into a different meaning.**

lessons.title: 写得热情一点，可以顺手许诺更多吗？
lessons.content:
# 写得热情一点，可以顺手许诺更多吗？

## 更热情的邀请，多出了一项安排

[2024年图书节记录](https://www.loc.gov/events/2024-national-book-festival)说明活动免费向公众开放，并介绍部分节目直播。你想把历史资料导览写得更亲切。

一段用于本课检查的编辑稿加上：“欢迎回顾，全部节目都能实时看。”这句话不是实际模型输出，也不是主办方的新公告。

## 先猜一下

这次改稿中，哪些是语气变化，哪些已经改变了需要来源支持的内容？

先写下你的判断，再往下看答案。

## 答案

“欢迎回顾”是在改变表达方式；把部分直播改成全部实时观看，则扩大了原公告的安排。更亲切不需要替主办方作出更多承诺。

## 只改变说话方式，先保住原来的条件

可以写：“没能到场也可以了解节目：原页面介绍了部分直播与会后录像安排。”你加入了面向读者的表达，却没有把“部分”改成“全部”。

向助手提出语气要求时，同时点名需要保留的事实。[请求写作指导](https://help.openai.com/en/articles/10032626-prompt-engineering-best-practices-for-chatgpt)中的语气与明确要求，可以一起使用。

:::detail[哪些词算语气，哪些词算新的事实？]
先看改动是否让读者对外部世界多相信了一件事。“欢迎回顾”“看看这份记录”主要改变你怎样招呼读者；“所有节目直播”“保证每场有字幕”则让读者相信主办方提供了具体服务。后者需要相应材料，不会因为整句话听起来友好就免于核对。边界有时与上下文有关，所以不要背一张永远适用的词表。把改前改后各读一遍，问这一处到底新增了什么可以被核实或反驳的安排。
:::

比较两种给定编辑规则，不预测任何模型的必然行为。看看在原句带有限定词时，它们会留下怎样不同的意思。

::play{#tone-without-changing-the-promise-contrast}

## 新增安排，先找到新增依据

如果你确实取得了另一份官方补充说明，可以把新信息加进导览，并保留对应入口。此时发生的不只是语气润色，而是有依据的内容更新。

:::detail[“免费活动”为什么不能顺手写成所有东西都免费？]
公开记录中的免费向公众开放，说明的是参加活动的门槛。它没有自动回答现场所有消费、交通、买书或其他服务的费用。你不需要在一段短导览里讨论每一项可能的开销，但也不能把范围扩大到原文没有说明的所有事情。若任务需要核对某一项费用，就去找那一项的具体说明。更全面的承诺不是更好的文案，它可能只是把还不知道的事情写得过于肯定。
:::

:::detail[怎样给出一条容易执行的修改意见？]
不要只说“写得不准确”。指出位置和要保留的边界，例如“把全部实时观看改回部分节目直播；保留友好的开头，不增加其他观看保证”。修改完后只看这一处条件是否恢复，再确认其他原有事实没有被改动。这样既不用把整段文字推倒重来，也不会因为喜欢新语气而接受新错误。你可以继续选择自己的表达风格，但事实变化与风格变化应当分别检查。把改动条件写在一句反馈里，下一版就有明确的比较对象，不必凭印象判断是否已经修好。
:::

## 自检

你只想把说明写得更鼓励人，稿子却出现“每段录像都有字幕”。准备保留这句之前，应该补查哪一项材料？

## 一句话

**语气可以更亲切，事实不能因此更夸张。**

en.title: If You Write More Enthusiastically, Can You Promise More Along the Way?
en.content:
# If You Write More Enthusiastically, Can You Promise More Along the Way?

## A Warmer Invitation That Adds an Extra Arrangement

The [2024 National Book Festival record](https://www.loc.gov/events/2024-national-book-festival) states that the event is free and open to the public, and describes livestreams for some programs. You want to make the guide to these historical materials sound friendlier.

An edited draft used for checking in this lesson adds: “Welcome back! You can watch all programs in real time.” This sentence is not actual model output, nor is it a new announcement from the organizers.

## Predict first
In this revision, which parts are changes in tone, and which have already changed content that requires source support?

Write down your judgment first before looking at the answer below.

## Answer
“Welcome back” changes the way things are phrased; changing some livestreams to watching all programs in real time expands what was arranged in the original announcement. Being friendlier does not require making more promises on behalf of the organizers.

## Change Only How You Say It; Keep the Original Conditions First

You could write: “Even if you couldn't attend in person, you can still explore the programs: the original page described arrangements for some livestreams and post-event recordings.” You added reader-facing phrasing without turning “some” into “all”.

When setting tone requirements for an assistant, also name the facts that must be preserved. Tone and explicit requirements from [requesting writing guidance](https://help.openai.com/en/articles/10032626-prompt-engineering-best-practices-for-chatgpt) can be used together.

:::detail[Which words count as tone, and which count as new facts?]
First check whether the change leads readers to believe one more thing about the external world. “Welcome back” and “take a look at this record” mainly change how you greet readers; “livestreaming all programs” and “guaranteed subtitles for every session” lead readers to believe the organizers provided specific services. The latter requires supporting material and is not exempt from verification just because the whole sentence sounds friendly. Boundaries sometimes depend on context, so do not memorize a word list meant to apply everywhere. Read the text before and after the edit, and ask what new arrangement was added here that could be verified or refuted.
:::

Compare two given editing rules without predicting what any model will inevitably do. See what different meanings they leave behind when the original sentence contains qualifiers.

::play{#tone-without-changing-the-promise-contrast}

## Adding New Arrangements: Find New Evidence First

If you have indeed obtained another official supplementary notice, you can add the new information into the guide while keeping the corresponding entry point. What is happening here is not just tone polishing, but an evidence-based content update.

:::detail[Why can't a "free event" casually be written as everything being free?]
Being free and open to the public in a public record describes the threshold for attending the event. It does not automatically answer for all on-site purchases, transportation, book purchases, or other service fees. You do not need to discuss every possible expense in a short guide, but you cannot expand the scope to everything not specified in the original text. If a task requires checking a specific fee, go find the specific explanation for that item. A more sweeping promise is not better copy; it may simply state things that are not yet known with too much certainty.
:::

:::detail[How do you give feedback for revision that is easy to execute?]
Do not simply say “this is inaccurate.” Point out the location and the boundary to preserve—for example, “change watching all programs in real time back to livestreaming some programs; keep the friendly opening, but do not add other viewing guarantees.” After revising, check only whether this condition has been restored, and then confirm that other original facts have not been altered. That way, you avoid tearing down and restarting the entire passage, and you avoid accepting new errors just because you like the new tone. You can continue choosing your own expressive style, but factual changes and stylistic changes should be checked separately. Stating the revision conditions in a single piece of feedback gives the next version a clear benchmark for comparison, so you do not have to judge from impression whether it has been fixed.
:::

## Check yourself
You only intended to make the description more encouraging, but the draft ended up saying “subtitles are provided for every recording.” Before preparing to keep this sentence, which piece of supporting material should you check?

## In one sentence
**Tone can be friendlier, but facts must not become more exaggerated as a result.**

lessons.title: 还缺一个细节，是补写还是先问？
lessons.content:
# 还缺一个细节，是补写还是先问？

## 读者问的细节，这一段里没有

你查看[2024年图书节的公开介绍](https://www.loc.gov/events/2024-national-book-festival)，在当前选用的这段材料中没有找到某场次具体的字幕安排。你的读者恰好关心这一点。

你准备请助手写一条询问草稿，或先完成一张只列已有信息的历史资料卡；现在不会真的向主办方发送消息。

## 先猜一下

怎样把这个缺口写出来，才不会把“还没找到”变成“确定没有”？

先写下你的判断，再往下看答案。

## 答案

说明你在当前材料中还没找到哪一项，再写一个具体可回答的询问。未知可以保留为待确认，不必为了填满资料卡而猜出安排。

## 把缺口变成一个有对象的问题

可以写：“我在这份2024年介绍中没找到该场次录像的字幕说明。请问可以在哪里查到？”它同时说明材料、对象和需要的下一步。

先把问题写清楚，再决定是否需要另找资料或联系相关方。你不是在替主办方宣布服务不存在。

:::detail[只说“有没有字幕”，为什么有时仍不够具体？]
一场图书节可能包含不同节目与不同观看方式。你问的是现场字幕、直播字幕，还是会后某段录像的字幕，回答可能需要不同的材料。把对象写清楚，可以减少对方猜测，也让你更容易判断答复是否真的解决问题。[W3C的写作提示](https://www.w3.org/WAI/tips/writing/)强调清楚表达目的与指令；用到询问中，就是给对方一个能够定位并回答的问题，而不是让他从整场活动里猜出你所指的部分。
:::

缺的同一项信息，在不同任务中是否必须先补齐？

::play{#a-question-not-an-invention-weigh}

## 什么时候该反过来

这项缺口不影响当前成品时，可以先完成已有事实，明确留下待确认项。若它直接决定读者能否使用这份导览，则先补查，再把结论写进去。

:::detail[怎样判断这项未知是否真的挡住任务？]
回到读者的目的。你只整理当年活动的日期与地点，某段录像的字幕状态不一定需要出现在成品里；你正在帮助依赖字幕的读者找到能使用的内容，这一项就直接影响导览是否有用。不是每个未知都必须立即解决，也不是所有未知都可以忽略。先判断它与当前用途的关系，就知道该暂停哪一步，或怎样把尚未确认的部分与已有结果分开交付。
:::

:::detail[在一个页面里没搜到，可以写整个网站都没有吗？]
不能把有限检查扩大成完整搜索结论。你可以如实写“这段介绍中未找到”或“这次查阅还没有确认”，并保留查过的入口。若继续查到另一份说明，就更新对应字段。明确检查范围不是给自己找借口，而是告诉接手的人下一步该补什么；“肯定没有”却会让别人以为这项调查已经结束。对于历史资料，还要注意后来发布的说明与当时公告可能处于不同时间，引用时各自标清。
:::

## 自检

读者改问某一种语言的字幕，而你只找到“提供字幕”这句话。你会怎样写下一条询问，避免把语言也擅自补上？

## 一句话

**没有找到的细节，先变成明确的问题，不变成编造的答案。**

en.title: Still Missing a Detail: Fill It In or Ask First?
en.content:
# Still Missing a Detail: Fill It In or Ask First?

## The Detail the Reader Asked About Is Not in This Excerpt

You check the [public overview of the 2024 National Book Festival](https://www.loc.gov/events/2024-national-book-festival) and do not find the specific caption arrangements for a certain session in the excerpt currently selected. Your reader happens to care about this.

You plan to ask an assistant to draft an inquiry, or first complete a historical reference card that lists only existing information; you will not actually send a message to the organizer right now.

## Predict first
How can you describe this gap without turning "not found yet" into "definitely does not exist"?

Write down your judgment first, then look below for the answer.

## Answer
State which item you have not yet found in the current material, and then write a specific, answerable inquiry. Unknowns can be left as pending confirmation; there is no need to guess an arrangement just to fill out the reference card.

## Turn the Gap into a Targeted Question

You could write: "I did not find caption information for this session's recording in this 2024 overview. Where can I find that?" This identifies the material, the specific subject, and the needed next step all at once.

Write the question clearly first, then decide whether you need to find additional sources or contact the relevant parties. You are not announcing on the organizer's behalf that the service does not exist.

:::detail[Why is just asking "are there captions" sometimes still not specific enough?]
A book festival may include different programs and different viewing methods. Whether you are asking about live captions, livestream captions, or captions for a post-event recording, answering may require different materials. Making the subject clear reduces guesswork for the other party and makes it easier for you to judge whether their reply actually solves your problem. [W3C writing tips](https://www.w3.org/WAI/tips/writing/) emphasize expressing purpose and instructions clearly; applied to an inquiry, this means giving the other party a question they can locate and answer, rather than making them guess which part of the entire event you mean.
:::

Must the same missing piece of information be filled in first across different tasks?

::play{#a-question-not-an-invention-weigh}

## When to choose the other way

When this gap does not affect the current deliverable, you can finish the established facts first and clearly leave pending items marked. If it directly determines whether the reader can use the guide, investigate it first before writing the conclusion in.

:::detail[How do you judge whether this unknown actually blocks the task?]
Return to the reader's goal. If you are only compiling the dates and locations of that year's event, the caption status of a particular recording does not necessarily need to appear in the deliverable; if you are helping readers who rely on captions find usable content, this item directly affects whether the guide is useful. Not every unknown must be resolved immediately, nor can all unknowns be ignored. Judge its relationship to the current use first, and you will know which step to pause, or how to deliver unconfirmed parts separately from established results.
:::

:::detail[If you didn't find it on one page, can you write that the entire website doesn't have it?]
You cannot broaden a limited check into a complete search conclusion. You can write truthfully, "not found in this introduction" or "not yet confirmed in this review," and keep a record of the sources you checked. If you later find another note, update the corresponding field. Defining the scope of your check clearly is not making excuses for yourself; it tells the person taking over what needs to be supplemented next. Claiming "definitely none," however, makes others assume the investigation is already finished. For historical materials, also note that statements released later and announcements made at the time may come from different dates, so label each clearly when citing.
:::

## Check yourself
The reader instead asks about captions in a specific language, but you only found the phrase "captions provided." How would you write the next inquiry to avoid making up a language on your own?

## In one sentence
**Turn details you have not found into clear questions first, not fabricated answers.**

lessons.title: 标题和链接写得漂亮，人就知道该点哪里吗？
lessons.content:
# 标题和链接写得漂亮，人就知道该点哪里吗？

## 只看链接文字，你知道会去哪里吗？

[W3C的功能图片示例](https://www.w3.org/WAI/tutorials/images/functional/)把打印与搜索图标按动作说明，而不是只说图标长什么样。再看你给[2024年图书节](https://www.loc.gov/events/2024-national-book-festival)做的资料卡：原始活动说明、节目资料以及你自己的导览，不是同一个入口。

如果几个链接都写“点击这里”，读者需要逐个打开才能知道里面是什么。

## 先猜一下

你会怎样给这些入口命名，让读者在点击前就知道自己要找哪一个？

先写下你的判断，再往下看答案。

## 答案

写出入口的目的或实际动作，例如查看活动说明、查找节目资料。链接文字是在帮助人选择，不只是装饰一串地址。

## 名字先说明这是什么入口

给原始活动页面写“查看2024年活动说明”，比只写“这里”更容易判断去向。给一份下载文件写“下载资料卡”，则要确认这个链接真的提供下载，而不是只打开介绍页。

### 同一个图标，动作可能不同

一个画着打印机的按钮，作用若是打印页面，名称就说明打印；一个画着放大镜的按钮，作用若是提交搜索，就说明搜索。不要让读者只能凭图形猜测。

:::detail[为什么不把所有链接都写成很短的“更多”？]
短不等于清楚。孤立地看“更多”，读者不知道是更多活动背景、更多节目，还是你的编辑说明。一个有目的的链接文字也可以很短，例如“查看活动说明”，同时告诉读者点开后大概会得到什么。[W3C的写作提示](https://www.w3.org/WAI/tips/writing/)把有意义的链接列为可访问写作的一部分；这里不要求你记住标准编号，只要把每个入口放回读者当前需要完成的动作。
:::

:::detail[只把图标描述得更详细，为什么还不够？]
“一个带手柄的放大镜”说明外观，却没有告诉使用者这个控件会做什么。功能图片需要传达动作或目的；展示作品的图片，则可能需要说明画面内容。两种情况的文字不是越详细越好，而是要匹配用途。你设计自己的资料卡时也一样：作品图注可以描述图中关系，查看原始资料的按钮则说明去向。把图片内容与按钮动作分开，读者不必先认识某种图标风格才能继续操作。
:::

给实际动作与入口名称配对。这里不发送表单，也不替任何人完成报名。

::play{#help-the-reader-find-the-action-sort}

## 它不是什么

入口名称不是一个可以提前宣告成功的地方。“查看报名说明”不等于“已经报名”；“打开录像页面”不等于保证所有录像已经上线。只命名这一步真正提供的动作。

:::detail[怎样检查自己命名的链接是否靠谱？]
先只读文字，写下你预期会发生的事，再实际打开链接比较。若写的是下载却只到了介绍页，改名或更换正确入口；若写的是原始记录，却到了自己的摘要，要说明这是摘要并另给原文。链接可打开只是第一层，目标是否符合名称还要另查。为历史活动做导览时，不要仅凭当年的录像计划就把每个节目写成已可播放；你查到了哪一步，就让名称表达哪一步。
:::

## 自检

一张卡片同时有原始网页、你写的摘要和可下载文件。怎样让不看图标的人只凭文字区分三者？

## 一句话

**入口文字说明实际去向与动作，不替尚未发生的事情宣布成功。**

en.title: If headings and links are nicely written, do people know where to click?
en.content:
# If headings and links are nicely written, do people know where to click?

## Looking only at the link text, do you know where it will lead?

[W3C's functional image examples](https://www.w3.org/WAI/tutorials/images/functional/) explain print and search icons by action rather than merely describing what the icons look like. Now look at the resource card you made for the [2024 Book Festival](https://www.loc.gov/events/2024-national-book-festival): the original event description, program materials, and your own guide are not the same entry point.

If several links all say "Click here", readers have to open them one by one to find out what is inside.

## Predict first
How would you label these entry points so that readers know which one they are looking for before clicking?

Write down your judgment first, then scroll down to see the answer.

## Answer
State the purpose or actual action of the entry point, such as viewing the event description or searching for program materials. Link text helps people make choices, rather than just decorating a URL string.

## Let the label first explain what kind of entry point this is

Writing "View 2024 event description" for the original event page makes it easier to judge the destination than just writing "here". Writing "Download resource card" for a downloadable file requires confirming that this link actually provides a download, rather than only opening an introduction page.

### The same icon may perform different actions

If a button with a printer icon serves to print the page, its label should explain printing; if a button with a magnifying glass icon serves to submit a search, it should explain searching. Do not leave readers to guess solely from the graphic.

:::detail[Why not write every link as a very short "More"?]
Short does not mean clear. Looking at "More" in isolation, readers do not know whether it means more event background, more programs, or your editorial notes. Purposeful link text can also be short, such as "View event description", while telling readers roughly what they will get after clicking. [W3C's writing tips](https://www.w3.org/WAI/tips/writing/) list meaningful links as part of accessible writing; you are not required to memorize standard numbers here, just place each entry point back into the action the reader currently needs to complete.
:::

:::detail[Why is only describing an icon in more detail still not enough?]
"A magnifying glass with a handle" describes appearance, but does not tell users what this control will do. Functional images need to convey action or purpose; images displaying artwork, on the other hand, may need to describe the visual content. For both situations, text is not better simply by being more detailed; rather, it must match the intended use. The same applies when you design your own resource cards: artwork captions can describe relationships in the picture, while buttons for viewing original sources explain the destination. By separating image content from button actions, readers do not need to recognize a particular icon style before proceeding.
:::

Pair actual actions with entry labels. This does not submit forms or complete registration for anyone.

::play{#help-the-reader-find-the-action-sort}

## What it is not

An entry label is not a place to declare success in advance. "View registration instructions" does not equal "Already registered"; "Open video page" does not equal guaranteeing that all videos are already online. Only name the action that this step actually provides.

:::detail[How do you check whether the links you labeled are reliable?]
First read only the text, write down what you expect to happen, and then actually open the link to compare. If it says download but only leads to an introduction page, rename it or switch to the correct entry point; if it says original record but leads to your own summary, explain that it is a summary and provide the original text separately. That a link can be opened is only the first layer; whether the destination matches the label requires separate checking. When creating a guide for historical events, do not write every program as already playable based solely on the video plans of that year; let the label express whichever step you have verified.
:::

## Check yourself
A card has the original webpage, your written summary, and a downloadable file all at the same time. How can you enable someone who does not look at icons to distinguish among the three using text alone?

## In one sentence
**Entry text states the actual destination and action, without declaring success for what has not yet happened.**

lessons.title: 这份短通知，可以交给陌生人了吗？
lessons.content:
# 这份短通知，可以交给陌生人了吗？

## 现在写一段真的能使用的短导览

回到[2024年图书节记录](https://www.loc.gov/events/2024-national-book-festival)。这次读者没有到场，想知道当时如何远程了解节目，也想保留原页面继续查阅。

你已有足够材料开始：这是2024年8月24日的活动；原介绍说明部分节目直播，并计划会后提供全部节目录像。你还没有逐一验证每段录像的实际交付状态。

## 先猜一下

你会怎样把这些材料写成两句导览，让读者既知道下一步，又不会误解你已经核对过的范围？

先写下你的判断，再往下看答案。

## 答案

说明历史活动身份与两种观看安排，再给一个名称清楚的原始入口。把公告中的计划与自己实际查看过的结果分开，不把还没查过的录像写成全部已可播放。

## 自己写，再按四个条件检查

先写你的两句话，不必模仿一份标准范文。检查四件事：年份清楚、读者目的得到回答、直播与录像范围没被改强、入口名称对应原始页面。

有AI工具时，可以请它针对这四项检查你的稿子；没有工具，也能直接拿原文逐项比较。学习成果是你的导览与检查，不是一次虚构的模型调用。

:::detail[为什么这里不给唯一的标准成稿？]
同一份真实材料可以写成不同的好导览。你可以先说没能到场的人怎样查看资料，也可以先交代这是哪一年的活动；只要事实范围准确、读者知道下一步，就不必与某一段范文逐字相同。这个任务练的是组织材料与检查条件，不是模仿作者的文风。可以把自己的第一版保留下来，标出哪一处根据原文修改过；之后再换一种读者需求，看看你是否还知道该保留什么。
:::

检查快完成的文字时，先处理真正影响这位读者使用的地方。

::play{#finish-a-clear-message-weigh}

## 什么时候该反过来

写到一项当前材料没有给出的具体节目状态，就先把那一项缩回已知范围，或去补查。不要为了完成两句话而给未知内容下结论；也不用因此把已经准确的全部文字删除。

:::detail[发现一处不确定，为什么不必重写整个作品？]
先定位这项不确定影响哪一句。若只是不知道某段录像是否已提供，可以把“已经上线”改回“原公告计划会后提供”，或者去实际核对那一段的当前入口。其他已确认的年份与活动身份仍可保留。小范围修正让你看清改了什么，也减少把原本正确的部分一起改坏的机会。完成后，再按整份小清单复查一遍，确认修改没有让另一个条件消失。
:::

:::detail[一个陌生人只看到文字，没有看到配图，仍能用吗？]
把配图遮住再读一遍：是否知道这是2024年的资料、远程观看有哪些不同方式、该到哪个入口继续查看？[W3C的写作提示](https://www.w3.org/WAI/tips/writing/)强调清楚的目的与结构，可以帮助你做这种检查。图片可以增添理解，但不应是唯一承载关键动作的地方。你不需要保证所有读者都觉得同样有趣；先保证这段短文在没有你现场解释时仍能完成自己承诺的小任务。
:::

## 自检

换成一位只想查某场节目的人，重新写两句话。哪些内容需要具体到场次，哪些仍可沿用这次的检查方法？

## 一句话

**一段可交付的短文，让读者知道做什么，也知道依据到哪里为止。**

en.title: Is This Short Notice Ready to Hand to a Stranger?
en.content:
# Is This Short Notice Ready to Hand to a Stranger?

## Now write a short guide that can actually be used

Return to the [2024 National Book Festival record](https://www.loc.gov/events/2024-national-book-festival). This time, the reader did not attend in person. They want to know how people could follow the programs remotely back then, and also want to keep the original page to consult further.

You have enough material to start: this was an event on August 24, 2024; the original description notes that some programs were livestreamed, and that recordings of all programs were planned to be provided after the event. You have not yet verified the actual delivery status of each individual recording.

## Predict first
How would you turn this material into a two-sentence guide so that readers know what to do next without misunderstanding the scope of what you have actually verified?

Write down your judgment first before looking down at the answer.

## Answer
State the past event's identity and the two viewing arrangements, then provide a clearly named original entry point. Separate the plan in the announcement from the results you actually checked yourself, and do not describe recordings you have not yet checked as all being ready to play.

## Write your own, then check against four criteria

Write your two sentences first; you don't need to imitate a standard model answer. Check four things: the year is clear, the reader's goal is answered, the scope of livestreams and recordings has not been overstated, and the entry name corresponds to the original page.

When you have an AI tool, you can ask it to check your draft against these four items; without tools, you can also compare directly against the original text item by item. The learning outcome is your guide and your check, not a fabricated model call.

:::detail[Why is no single standard final draft provided here?]
The same real material can be written into different good guides. You could start by explaining how someone who could not attend in person can view the materials, or you could start by stating which year the event took place. As long as the scope of facts is accurate and the reader knows what to do next, your draft does not need to match a particular model text word for word. This task practices organizing material and checking criteria, not imitating an author's writing style. You can keep your first version and mark which parts were revised based on the original text; later, try switching to a different reader need to see whether you still know what to retain.
:::

When checking text that is nearly finished, first handle what truly affects how this reader uses it.

::play{#finish-a-clear-message-weigh}

## When to choose the other way

If you write about a specific program status that the current material does not provide, scale that item back to the known scope first, or go verify it. Don't jump to conclusions about unknown details just to finish two sentences; nor do you need to delete all the text that is already accurate.

:::detail[When you find an uncertainty, why don't you need to rewrite the entire piece?]
First locate which sentence this uncertainty affects. If you simply do not know whether a certain recording is already available, you can change "is now online" back to "the original announcement planned to provide it after the event," or actually check that segment's current entry point. Other confirmed details, such as the year and event identity, can still be kept. Making small-scale corrections lets you see clearly what changed and reduces the risk of breaking parts that were already correct. Once finished, recheck against the entire short checklist to confirm that the modification did not cause another condition to disappear.
:::

:::detail[If a stranger only sees the text without the images, can they still use it?]
Cover the images and read it again: does the reader know this is material from 2024, what different ways there are to watch remotely, and which entry point to go to for further reading? [W3C's writing tips](https://www.w3.org/WAI/tips/writing/) emphasize clear purpose and structure, which can help you perform this kind of check. Images can enhance understanding, but they should not be the only place carrying key actions. You don't need to guarantee that every reader finds it equally interesting; first ensure that this short text can fulfill the modest task it promises even without you there to explain it in person.
:::

## Check yourself
Switch to a reader who only wants to look up a specific program, and rewrite the two sentences. Which details need to be specific to that session, and which can still follow the checking method from this lesson?

## In one sentence
**A deliverable short text lets readers know what to do, and where the evidence ends.**

lessons.title: 只找发布日期，也要先读一篇长摘要吗？
lessons.content:
# 只找发布日期，也要先读一篇长摘要吗？

## 只想知道哪天发布，却收到一篇介绍

[由史密森尼管理的开放数据集条目](https://registry.opendata.aws/smithsonian-open-access/)记录了一次具体发布：2020年2月25日开放超过280万件二维、三维图像及相关数据。条目还介绍了机构馆藏、许可和更新方式。

你这次只需要给时间轴填发布日，准备让AI帮助处理这份公开材料。

## 先猜一下

怎样写请求，才能先拿到你真正要填的那一个字段？

先写下你的判断，再往下看答案。

## 答案

明确要求提取发布事件的日期，并指出支持它的原句位置。只有想了解整个项目时，才需要把多项信息组织成摘要。

## 给要找的信息起一个准确名字

可以请求：“只提取这次开放发布的年月日，注明它对应的事件；未找到就写未提供。”这把发布日期与页面查看时间分开了。

[文件上传说明](https://help.openai.com/en/articles/8555545)区分提取、转换和综合。对你的任务，先选要做的动作，比先要求一篇全面报告更有用。

:::detail[为什么不能只说“把日期找出来”？]
一个页面可能同时包含机构成立时间、一次发布的日期，和你自己打开页面的时间。你要填的是开放发布事件，不能只取第一串数字或最近的年份。给字段加上动作，就让提取目标更清楚。结果回来以后仍要看原句中的主语与动作是否匹配；格式整齐的表格，也不能替你证明选对了日期。若页面没有自己发布日期的标记，也不能拿事件日期顺便填上那个不同字段。
:::

两位读者面对同一个真实条目，先选择适合各自任务的输出。

::play{#choose-summary-or-extraction-weigh}

## 什么时候该反过来

读者想知道开放计划是什么、能做什么、在哪里继续查，才需要把相关信息综合成一段导览。你可以先提取字段，再综合；两种动作不必互相排斥。

:::detail[让AI只给一个字段，会不会丢掉上下文？]
所以请求中可以保留很短的支持说明，例如日期所对应的事件和原始入口。你得到的是一项有依据的数据，不是一篇长文，也不是一个脱离材料的裸数字。需要检查时可以回到那一句，之后再决定是否展开背景。这种分层适合整理许多资料：先把要对齐的字段找准，再做比较或总结。不要因为输出短，就省略字段含义；简洁与可核对可以同时做到。
:::

:::detail[摘要里也有日期，为什么还要区分？]
摘要可能正确包含那一天，但它的目标是挑选和组织主要内容，不保证把你需要的每个字段都按相同格式列出。你随后还要从长文里找一遍。明确提取字段，能减少这一步转手；要写项目介绍时，反过来只给日期又不够。判断哪种输出更好，要看你马上要用它完成什么，而不是把长摘要自动当成更认真、更专业的回答。
:::

## 自检

现在表格只缺数据集的管理者，不再缺发布日。你会怎样把请求改成一个能核对的字段？

## 一句话

**先确定要提取什么，再决定是否需要一篇摘要。**

en.title: Even if you only need the release date, do you still have to read a long summary first?
en.content:
# Even if you only need the release date, do you still have to read a long summary first?

## You only want to know the release date, but receive an overview instead

[The open dataset entry managed by the Smithsonian](https://registry.opendata.aws/smithsonian-open-access/) records a specific release: on February 25, 2020, more than 2.8 million 2D and 3D images and associated data were made open access. The entry also covers the institution's collection, licensing, and update methods.

This time, you only need to fill in the release date on a timeline, and you plan to have AI help process this public material.

## Predict first
How should you write your prompt to get just the single field you actually need to fill in first?

Write down your judgment first before looking at the answer below.

## Answer
Explicitly request the date of the release event and ask for the location of the supporting original sentence. Only when you want to understand the entire project do you need to organize multiple pieces of information into a summary.

## Give the target information an accurate name

You could prompt: "Extract only the year, month, and day of this open release, noting its corresponding event; if not found, write 'Not provided'." This separates the release date from the time the page was viewed.

The [file upload instructions](https://help.openai.com/en/articles/8555545) distinguish between extraction, transformation, and synthesis. For your task, choosing the action you want to take first is more useful than asking for a comprehensive report right away.

:::detail[Why can't you just say "find the date"?]
A single page might contain the founding date of the institution, the date of a specific release, and the timestamp of when you opened the page. What you need to fill in is the open release event, so you cannot simply grab the first string of numbers or the most recent year. Attaching an action to the field makes your extraction target clearer. Once the result comes back, you still need to check whether the subject and action in the original sentence match; a neatly formatted table cannot prove on its own that you picked the right date. If the page lacks a timestamp for its own publication date, you also cannot simply use the event date to fill in that different field.
:::

Two readers face the same real entry, each first choosing the output suited to their respective task.

::play{#choose-summary-or-extraction-weigh}

## When to choose the other way

Only when readers want to know what the open initiative is, what it enables, and where to look further do they need to synthesize the relevant information into an overview guide. You can extract fields first and synthesize later; the two actions do not have to be mutually exclusive.

:::detail[If you have AI provide only a single field, will you lose context?]
This is why you can keep a very brief supporting note in your prompt, such as the event corresponding to the date and the original passage. What you get is a grounded data point, not a lengthy text, nor a bare number detached from the source material. When you need to verify it, you can return to that specific sentence before deciding whether to expand on the background. This layered approach works well for organizing large amounts of material: first pinpoint the fields that need alignment, then compare or summarize. Do not omit the meaning of the field just because the output is short; conciseness and verifiability can be achieved at the same time.
:::

:::detail[A summary also contains dates, so why distinguish between them?]
A summary may correctly include that day, but its goal is to select and organize the main content; it does not guarantee that every field you need will be listed in a uniform format. You would then have to comb through the long text a second time. Explicitly extracting fields reduces this extra pass-through; conversely, when you need to write a project introduction, providing only a date is not enough. Deciding which output is better depends on what you need to accomplish right away, rather than automatically treating a long summary as a more diligent or professional response.
:::

## Check yourself
Now the table is only missing the dataset maintainer, no longer the release date. How would you adjust the prompt into a verifiable field?

## In one sentence
**Determine what you need to extract first, then decide whether you need a summary.**

lessons.title: 图像、图书和档案，能都填进“人数”吗？
lessons.content:
# 图像、图书和档案，能都填进“人数”吗？

## 几串大数字，数的却不是同一种东西

[史密森尼的数据集条目](https://registry.opendata.aws/smithsonian-open-access/)把开放发布的超过280万件图像，与机构背景中的1.55亿件物品、210万册图书、15.6万立方英尺档案分别说明。

你想让AI把它们整理成小表。表头暂时只有“数字”和“人数”，所有内容都等着往里面填。

## 先猜一下

你会先改哪些列名，才能让表格保留这些数字真正的含义？

先写下你的判断，再往下看答案。

## 答案

分别记录数的是什么、数值与限定词、单位、对应时点以及来源。不能因为它们都很大，就把图像、图书和空间体积一律写成人数。

## 一行装一项清楚的记录

先写一行：“开放发布图像｜超过280万｜件｜2020年2月25日发布事件｜数据集说明。”再给图书另起一行，保留“册”，并标明条目没有为这项机构背景数单独给统计日期。

[数据分析说明](https://help.openai.com/en/articles/8437071)提供整理与查看数据的工具；列名是否正确，仍需要你对照材料决定。

:::detail[“一行一事件”是说每行都必须有精确年月日吗？]
不是。它提醒你一行只表达一项可以说清的记录，时间不明时也如实留下。发布图像那一行有明确事件日；背景中的图书总量没有单独标统计时点，就不应该沿用上一行的日期。复制表格时最容易把空格自动补齐，看起来规整，却把不同记录绑在了同一天。你可以写“本条未给单独统计时点”，这比一个未经材料支持的日期更方便接手的人继续核查。
:::

:::detail[图像和物品都写“件”，就能相加吗？]
计量词相同不代表对象相同。一件馆藏物品可以有多个视角的数字图像，数字资料也可能包含不同类型的记录；你需要先知道集合之间如何对应，才能谈合计。当前条目把开放数据与机构背景分别叙述，并没有提供一一对应表。把对象名称保留在每一行，让读者不至于只看到一个“件”字就把它们加起来。遇到没有对应关系的信息，先保留不同记录，不制造一个无法解释的总数。
:::

:::detail[怎样检查AI整理出的表，不必重新读完每一段？]
先抽查每一行是否带着对象与单位，再把关键数字回指到原句。发现某一行把立方英尺写成件，先修正那一行，同时查是否还有同类复制错误。不要只确认数字抄对：15.6万旁边的单位变了，整条记录就已经变了。表格的好处是让问题更容易定位，前提是列名没有把原来不同的事情压成一个模糊类别。最后保留来源入口，下次更新才知道去哪找。
:::

把真实条目中的数量放回正确对象；这里没有一项是在统计使用人数。

::play{#one-row-one-event-sort}

## 自检

你准备加入[本次项目页](https://www.si.edu/openaccess)的“超过510万件数字项目”记录。需要补上哪些列，才不会被误认为2020年那次发布的精确数量？

## 一句话

**数字、对象、单位与时点一起保存，表格才不会改变材料的意思。**

en.title: Can Images, Books, and Archives All Be Put into "Headcount"?
en.content:
# Can Images, Books, and Archives All Be Put into "Headcount"?

## Several Large Numbers, but Not Counting the Same Thing

The [Smithsonian dataset entry](https://registry.opendata.aws/smithsonian-open-access/) explains the more than 2.8 million openly released images separately from the institutional background's 155 million items, 2.1 million books, and 156,000 cubic feet of archives.

You want an AI to organize them into a small table. For now, the headers only have "Number" and "Headcount," and all the content is waiting to be filled in.

## Predict first
Which column names would you change first so that the table preserves the true meaning of these numbers?

Write down your judgment first before reading the answer below.

## Answer
Record separately what is being counted, the value and qualifiers, the unit, the corresponding point in time, and the source. Just because they are all large, you cannot write images, books, and spatial volume uniformly as headcount.

## One Clear Record per Row

First write a row: "Openly released images | More than 2.8 million | items | February 25, 2020 release event | Dataset description." Then start a new row for the books, keep "volumes," and note that the entry does not provide an individual statistics date for this institutional background figure.

The [data analysis guide](https://help.openai.com/en/articles/8437071) provides tools for organizing and viewing data; whether the column names are correct still requires you to decide against the source material.

:::detail[Does "one row, one event" mean every row must have an exact year, month, and day?]
No. It reminds you that a row expresses only one record that can be clearly stated, and when the time is unclear, leave it as such truthfully. The row for releasing images has a clear event date; the total number of books in the background does not have an individually marked point in time for the statistics, so it should not carry over the date from the previous row. When copying tables, it is easiest to automatically fill in blanks; it looks neat, but binds different records to the same day. You can write "No individual point in time for statistics provided in this entry," which makes it easier for the next person to continue verifying than a date unsupported by the source material.
:::

:::detail[If images and items are both written as "items," can they be added together?]
Identical counting units do not mean identical objects. A single collection item can have digital images from multiple angles, and digital materials may also include different types of records; you need to know how the sets correspond to each other before you can talk about totaling them. The current entry describes open data and institutional background separately and does not provide a one-to-one correspondence table. Keeping the object name in each row prevents readers from adding them together just because they see the word "items." When encountering information without a correspondence relationship, keep the distinct records for now, and do not manufacture an unexplainable total.
:::

:::detail[How can you check a table organized by AI without having to reread every paragraph?]
First spot-check whether each row carries an object and a unit, then trace the key numbers back to their original sentences. If you discover that a row wrote cubic feet as items, fix that row first while checking whether there are other similar copying errors. Do not just confirm that the number was copied correctly: once the unit next to 156,000 changes, the entire record has changed. The advantage of a table is that it makes issues easier to locate, provided that the column names have not compressed originally different things into a single vague category. Finally, preserve the source access point so you know where to look during the next update.
:::

Place the quantities from the real entry back onto their correct objects; none of these is counting user headcount.

::play{#one-row-one-event-sort}

## Check yourself
You plan to add the record of "more than 5.1 million digital items" from [this project page](https://www.si.edu/openaccess). Which columns need to be added so that it will not be mistaken for the exact quantity from that 2020 release?

## In one sentence
**Keep numbers, objects, units, and points in time together so the table does not alter the meaning of the material.**

lessons.title: 两个数字放在一起，就能比出进展吗？
lessons.content:
# 两个数字放在一起，就能比出进展吗？

## 280万和510万，下一步就是算增幅吗？

[数据集条目](https://registry.opendata.aws/smithsonian-open-access/)记录2020年开放发布超过280万件图像；[项目主页](https://www.si.edu/openaccess)在本课查阅时写着超过510万件二维、三维数字项目。

你打算请AI计算这两个数字之间的精确增长率。两个材料里的数值都有“超过”，对象名称也并不完全相同。

## 先猜一下

开始计算之前，你还需要确认哪些条件，才能知道这次比较说明什么？

先写下你的判断，再往下看答案。

## 答案

先对齐对象、范围、时点与数值精度。两个下限不能直接给出精确增幅；图像与数字项目的对应范围，也需要查清再比较。

## 只看数字，容易把不同问题当成一个

计算器可以精确处理你输入的数，却不会替你判断输入是不是同一种统计。280万与510万在这里都是带限定的表述，不是两份逐项清点的精确总数。

你可以先写“两个页面分别报告了这些范围”，而不急着给出百分比。

:::detail[为什么两个“超过”不能相减成实际新增数？]
“超过280万”没有告诉你准确超过多少，“超过510万”也一样。把限定词删掉再相减，只算出了两个写在纸上的门槛之间的差，不是原本两项真实总量的差。即使后来确认统计对象一致，也还需要相应的精确值或可说明的估算方法，才能赋予结果那种含义。保留这点不确定不会让简报没有价值；它告诉读者目前能比较到哪一步，以及更深入计算缺少什么。
:::

比较两种检查规则：只转换数值，或同时检查它的对象与精度。给定结果是教学规则的结果，不是模型实测。

::play{#compare-the-same-thing-contrast}

## 先看对象，再决定能比哪一层

你也可以比较同一数字的中英文写法是否对应，或核对同一记录有没有抄错。这些问题不要求推算跨年份的增长。先说清比较目的，再选相应的依据。

:::detail[对齐了单位，为什么还要对齐时间？]
一份材料的当年新增数，与另一份材料的累计总量，即使用同一个计量单位，也回答不同问题。时间不仅是一个日期标签，还包括这是截至某时的总量，还是一段时间内发生的动作。当前数据集中的发布记录与项目主页中的访问规模，应该各自保留自己的来源身份。不能因为读者想看增长图，就把两者默默改成同一种年度统计。想做那种图，应补找定义一致、时期明确的数据。
:::

:::detail[没有足够数据，能不能先做一张比较表？]
可以，表格能用来展示差异，不一定非要排名或计算。把两份材料的用词、限定词和时点分别列出来，最后写“尚未核对统计范围是否一致”，就能帮助下一位读者继续查。你保留的是可检查的线索。相反，一张带小数点的增长图可能看起来更专业，却隐藏了数据不对齐的问题。先让表格说明自己知道什么，再考虑图表是否有一个真实可解释的数值关系。
:::

## 自检

一份新表报告当年新增图像，另一份报告截至年底所有图像。除了单位，还要怎样写清它们各自统计的时间范围？

## 一句话

**先确认在比同一种东西，再让计算服务这个比较。**

en.title: Can Putting Two Numbers Together Show Progress?
en.content:
# Can Putting Two Numbers Together Show Progress?

## 2.8 Million and 5.1 Million: Is the Next Step to Calculate Growth?

The [dataset entry](https://registry.opendata.aws/smithsonian-open-access/) records an open release of more than 2.8 million images in 2020; the [project homepage](https://www.si.edu/openaccess), when consulted for this lesson, stated more than 5.1 million 2D and 3D digital items.

You plan to ask an AI to calculate the exact growth rate between these two numbers. The values in both materials include "more than," and the names of the objects are not completely identical.

## Predict first
Before you start calculating, what conditions do you still need to confirm to know what this comparison actually shows?

Write down your judgment first before looking at the answer below.

## Answer
First align the objects, scope, points in time, and numerical precision. Two lower bounds cannot directly produce an exact growth rate; the corresponding scope between images and digital items also needs to be clarified before comparing.

## Looking Only at Numbers Makes It Easy to Treat Different Questions as One

A calculator can process the numbers you enter with precision, but it will not determine for you whether what you entered represents the same kind of statistic. Both 2.8 million and 5.1 million here are qualified statements, not two precise totals from item-by-item counts.

You can start by writing "the two pages reported these respective scopes," instead of rushing to provide a percentage.

:::detail[Why Can't Two "More Than" Numbers Be Subtracted to Find the Actual Increase?]
"More than 2.8 million" does not tell you exactly how much it exceeds, and neither does "more than 5.1 million." Removing the qualifiers and subtracting only calculates the difference between two thresholds written on paper, not the difference between the two original real totals. Even if it is later confirmed that the statistical objects are consistent, you still need corresponding exact values or an explainable estimation method to give the result that meaning. Preserving this uncertainty does not make the briefing valueless; it tells readers how far the comparison can currently go and what is missing for deeper calculations.
:::

Compare two checking rules: converting only numerical values, or simultaneously checking their objects and precision. The given results are the results of instructional rules, not actual model tests.

::play{#compare-the-same-thing-contrast}

## Look at the Object First, Then Decide What Level Can Be Compared

You can also compare whether two ways of writing the same number match, or check whether the same record was transcribed incorrectly. These questions do not require projecting multi-year growth. State the purpose of the comparison clearly first, then choose the corresponding basis.

:::detail[Once Units Are Aligned, Why Must Time Also Be Aligned?]
A source's new additions for the current year and another source's cumulative total answer different questions, even if they use the same unit of measurement. Time is not just a date tag; it also encompasses whether this is a cumulative total as of a certain time or an action that occurred over a period of time. The release records in the current dataset and the scale of access on the project homepage should each retain their own source identity. You cannot quietly turn both into the same kind of annual statistic just because readers want to see a growth chart. If you want to make that kind of chart, you should find additional data with consistent definitions and clear time periods.
:::

:::detail[If There Isn't Enough Data, Can You Make a Comparison Table First?]
Yes, tables can be used to show differences; they don't necessarily have to rank or calculate. Listing the phrasing, qualifiers, and points in time from both sources separately, and concluding with "statistical scope has not yet been verified for consistency," helps the next reader continue investigating. What you preserve are checkable clues. In contrast, a growth chart with decimals might look more professional, but it conceals the problem of unaligned data. First let the table explain what is known, and only then consider whether a chart possesses a genuinely explainable numerical relationship.
:::

## Check yourself
One new table reports images added during the year, while another reports all images as of the end of the year. Beyond the unit of measurement, how else should you clearly describe the time range each of them measures?

## In one sentence
**First confirm you are comparing the same thing, then let calculations serve that comparison.**

lessons.title: 表格里有空白，是不是就不够专业？
lessons.content:
# 表格里有空白，是不是就不够专业？

## 能访问多少资料，并没有回答用了多少人

[史密森尼项目主页](https://www.si.edu/openaccess)在本课查阅时说明可访问超过510万件数字项目。你准备给资料简报增加一列“独立使用人数”，却没有在选用的这段说明里找到这个数。

单元里的两份页面说明了资料规模和入口，不自动提供你想要的全部使用统计。

## 先猜一下

这一格怎样填写，才能让别人知道还缺什么，而不是误以为结果已经查明？

先写下你的判断，再往下看答案。

## 答案

标明当前选用材料未报告这个字段，并注明需要补查的统计对象与时期。空白不等于零，资料数量也不能代替人数。

## 给未知一个明确名字

写“独立使用人数：当前材料未报告；需另查同一时期、排除重复后的统计”，比留一个无人能解释的空格更有用。

不要把“超过510万件数字项目”搬进这一格。正确的数字放进错误的列，仍然是错误信息。

:::detail[写“没有数据”，与写“没有用户”差在哪里？]
前者是在说明这次资料整理没有得到那个字段，后者是在对真实使用情况作结论。即使你查了一个官方页面，也不能把它没报告的内容直接当成不存在。你可以记录查过哪一段、缺什么定义，然后转向适合的统计入口。项目主页提供使用统计入口，但你还没有核对到的数据，不能提前写成已取得的结果。把资料查阅的状态与现实中的数量分开，是填写这类表格时最重要的动作。
:::

:::detail[确实有一项数据等于零，怎样与未知区分？]
需要材料明确给出那个零，以及它统计的对象与时期。这样你才能写“报告为0”，而不是用0代替不知道。表格可以为未知保留一个文字状态，为明确记录保留数值，两者不要混用。在后续计算中，未知通常需要另作处理；把它当零会改变总数或平均值。这里先不用学公式，只要在交付资料时说明哪一格来自记录、哪一格仍待补查，就能避免接手的人把猜测算进结果。
:::

:::detail[别人要求每一格必须有东西，怎么办？]
可以填状态，而不是填一个不真实的数。例如“当前材料未报告”“对象定义待核对”“查阅入口不可用”都说明了不同问题，也指向不同的下一步。状态文字应当尽量具体：不要把技术上打不开页面与已读完却没有这个字段混为一谈。这样的表格不是不专业，而是让下一位使用者看清证据的边界。以后拿到新材料，再把对应状态替换成有来源的记录，而不是让旧猜测一直流传。
:::

把一条真实说明与几种资料整理状态分清。状态卡是本课的检查练习，不是额外的机构统计。

::play{#leave-gaps-visible-sort}

## 自检

后来另一个来源给出总下载动作，但仍未排除同一个人的重复行为。原来的独立人数空格是否已经有了合适的值？

## 一句话

**把未知写清楚，比用一个不对应的数字填满表格更可靠。**

en.title: Are Blank Cells in a Table Unprofessional?
en.content:
# Are Blank Cells in a Table Unprofessional?

## How Much Material Is Accessible Does Not Answer How Many People Used It

At the time it was consulted for this lesson, the [Smithsonian project homepage](https://www.si.edu/openaccess) stated that more than 5.1 million digital items were accessible. You are preparing to add a "Unique Users" column to an information briefing, but you did not find this number in the selected description.

The two pages in this unit describe the scale of the materials and how to access them, but they do not automatically provide all the usage statistics you want.

## Predict first
How should this cell be filled out so that others know what is still missing, rather than mistaking it for a verified result?

Write down your judgment first before looking at the answer below.

## Answer
Indicate that the currently selected material does not report this field, and note the statistical subject and time period that need follow-up checking. A blank does not equal zero, and the quantity of materials cannot replace the number of people.

## Give the Unknown a Clear Name

Writing "Unique users: not reported in current material; deduplicated statistics for the same period need to be checked separately" is more useful than leaving a blank cell that no one can explain.

Do not move "more than 5.1 million digital items" into this cell. A correct number put into the wrong column is still incorrect information.

:::detail[What is the difference between writing "No data" and writing "No users"?]
The former explains that this round of research did not obtain that field, while the latter draws a conclusion about actual usage. Even if you check an official page, you cannot assume that what it did not report simply does not exist. You can record which section was checked and what definition is missing, and then turn to a suitable statistics entry point. The project homepage provides an entry point for usage statistics, but data you have not yet verified cannot be recorded in advance as an established result. Separating the status of your research from real-world quantities is the most important step when filling out these types of tables.
:::

:::detail[If a data point really is zero, how do you distinguish it from the unknown?]
The material needs to explicitly provide that zero, along with the object and time period it measures. Only then can you write "reported as 0" rather than using 0 to stand in for the unknown. A table can preserve a text status for the unknown and keep numeric values for explicit records; do not mix the two. In subsequent calculations, unknowns usually require separate handling; treating them as zero alters totals or averages. You do not need to learn formulas here—simply explaining upon delivery which cells come from records and which cells still require follow-up checking will prevent whoever takes over from factoring guesswork into the results.
:::

:::detail[What should you do if someone requires every cell to be filled?]
You can enter a status instead of entering an untrue number. For example, "Not reported in current material," "Target definition needs verification," or "Access point unavailable" each explain different issues and point to different next steps. Status text should be as specific as possible: do not conflate a page that technically cannot be opened with one that was fully read but lacks this field. A table like this is not unprofessional; rather, it allows the next user to clearly see the boundaries of the evidence. When new materials are obtained later, you can replace the corresponding status with a sourced record, instead of letting old guesses circulate indefinitely.
:::

Distinguish a factual statement from several document review statuses. The status cards are a check exercise for this lesson, not additional institutional statistics.

::play{#leave-gaps-visible-sort}

## Check yourself
Later, another source provides the total number of download actions, but still does not exclude repeat actions by the same person. Does the original blank cell for unique users now have a suitable value?

## In one sentence
**Clearly stating what is unknown is more reliable than filling a table with a mismatched number.**

lessons.title: 这句话从哪里来，你还能找回去吗？
lessons.content:
# 这句话从哪里来，你还能找回去吗？

## 链接都放到末尾，哪一句来自哪一页？

你有两份真实来源：[数据集条目](https://registry.opendata.aws/smithsonian-open-access/)讲述2020年的开放发布，[项目主页](https://www.si.edu/openaccess)在本课查看时说明超过510万件数字项目及不同入口。

你把两句话合进一页简报，末尾只留“来源：史密森尼”。下一位读者想查其中一个数字，却不知道该从哪里开始。

## 先猜一下

你会给每条关键结论留下哪些线索，让别人能回到支持它的具体材料？

先写下你的判断，再往下看答案。

## 答案

让结论跟着自己的来源入口、对应位置和时间身份。机构名称相同，不代表任意一页都支持另外一页的所有信息。

## 从一句话，回到支撑它的位置

先把“2020年发布事件”指向数据集条目的说明段，再把“本次查看的数字项目规模”指向项目页开篇。两句各带自己的时间标签。

[NotebookLM的初始介绍](https://blog.google/innovation-and-ai/technology/ai/notebooklm-google-ai/)展示了依据提供材料生成解释与引用的设计。使用引用工具时，你仍要打开每个入口，核对对应句子。

:::detail[两个来源都来自同一机构，为什么还要分开？]
机构身份帮助你知道发布者，但具体页面才承载这次要引用的信息。一次发布记录与一个持续更新的项目入口，面向的用途和时间不同。读者想复查2020年发生的事情，不能只被送到今天的搜索首页；想了解本次可访问的资料入口，也不应只能看到历史公告。给每条结论一个能继续查的落点，就把机构的总体可信度转成了具体主张的可核查性。
:::

:::detail[链接能打开，就说明引用完成了吗？]
还要看页面是否真正支持旁边的结论。你写的是独立人数，打开的页面却只列数字项目件数，网络请求成功也没有解决这个问题。复查时按顺序看：链接到的是哪份材料、哪一段支持这句话、原文有没有你删掉的限定。能打开是可访问性，能支持是证据关系。把这两层分开，你就不会因为摘要带了很多蓝色链接，就把全部结论都当作已经确认。
:::

:::detail[后来移动或更换了来源页面，摘要还能用吗？]
先保留原来的标题、发布者、查看日期和对应位置记录，再查是否有可信的新入口。找到了同一材料的正式迁移页，可以更新链接并说明核对时间；没有找到，就如实保留访问问题，不能把相似标题的另一篇文章当成原文。若这一来源支撑的是核心结论，应在重新发布简报前补足可核查材料。旧引用的存在是线索，不是新入口已经核验的证明。
:::

把简报中两条真实信息送回支持它的页面；对没有取得的字段保留缺口。

::play{#a-summary-with-a-trail-sort}

## 自检

把两条结论复制到另一份文件时，怎样让它们各自的链接、时点和限定词继续留在一起？

## 一句话

**引用不是一份机构名单，而是每条结论回到材料的路径。**

en.title: Where Did This Statement Come From, and Can You Trace It Back?
en.content:
# Where Did This Statement Come From, and Can You Trace It Back?

## Links Are All at the End: Which Sentence Comes from Which Page?

You have two authentic sources: a [dataset entry](https://registry.opendata.aws/smithsonian-open-access/) describing the 2020 open-access release, and a [project homepage](https://www.si.edu/openaccess) that, when viewed for this lesson, notes more than 5.1 million digital items and various access points.

You combine two sentences into a one-page briefing, leaving only "Source: Smithsonian" at the end. The next reader wants to check one of the figures, but has no idea where to start.

## Predict first
What clues would you leave for each key conclusion so that others can trace it back to the specific material that supports it?

Write down your judgment first, then read on for the answer.

## Answer
Anchor each conclusion to its own source entry point, specific location, and time identity. Sharing an institutional name does not mean any given page supports all the information on another page.

## From a Sentence Back to the Location That Supports It

First, point the "2020 release event" to the descriptive paragraph of the dataset entry, then point the "scale of digital items viewed this time" to the opening of the project page. Give each sentence its own timestamp.

The [initial introduction to NotebookLM](https://blog.google/innovation-and-ai/technology/ai/notebooklm-google-ai/) showcases a design that generates explanations and citations based on provided materials. Even when using citation tools, you still need to open each access point and verify the corresponding sentence.

:::detail[If both sources come from the same institution, why separate them?]
An institution's identity helps you know the publisher, but the specific page is what carries the information you are citing this time. A one-time release record and an ongoing, updated project portal serve different purposes and timeframes. If readers want to verify what happened in 2020, they cannot simply be sent to today's search landing page; if they want to explore the access points available during this review, they shouldn't be shown only a historical announcement. Giving each conclusion a landing spot where investigation can continue turns the general credibility of an institution into the verifiability of a specific claim.
:::

:::detail[If a link opens, does that mean the citation is complete?]
You also need to check whether the page actually supports the conclusion beside it. If you wrote about the number of unique visitors, but the opened page only lists the number of digital items, a successful web request does not solve the problem. When verifying, review in order: which material is linked, which paragraph supports the statement, and whether the original source contains qualifiers you omitted. Being able to open the link is accessibility; being able to support the claim is an evidential relationship. Separating these two layers keeps you from assuming all conclusions are confirmed just because a summary has plenty of blue links.
:::

:::detail[If the source page is later moved or replaced, can the summary still be used?]
First retain the original title, publisher, access date, and record of the corresponding location, then check whether a credible new entry point exists. If you find the official migration page for the same material, you can update the link and note the verification time. If you cannot find one, record the access issue truthfully, rather than treating another article with a similar title as the original source. If this source supports a core conclusion, you should provide verifiable material before reissuing the briefing. The presence of an old citation is a clue, not proof that the new entry point has already been verified.
:::

Send the two pieces of factual information in the briefing back to the pages that support them; leave gaps for fields that were not obtained.

::play{#a-summary-with-a-trail-sort}

## Check yourself
When copying two conclusions into another document, how can you ensure their respective links, timestamps, and qualifiers remain together?

## In one sentence
**A citation is not a list of institutions, but a path for each conclusion back to its source material.**

en.locator: Description, Managed By, License and How to Cite
en.supports: The SI-managed dataset description records the February 25, 2020 release of over 2.8 million CC0 2-D and 3-D images with related metadata and research data. en.limitations: A living page checked on 2026-09-15, not a statement that the number will stay unchanged or that all images found online are reusable. Digital items, objects, downloads and people are not interchangeable. This is not a controlled outcome study.

lessons.title: 只给你一页，你会留下哪些信息？
lessons.content:
# 只给你一页，你会留下哪些信息？

## 给想做作品的人，一页资料就够起步

[史密森尼项目页](https://www.si.edu/openaccess)提供开放资料的搜索、三维内容和学习资源入口；[数据集条目](https://registry.opendata.aws/smithsonian-open-access/)说明所述开放数据及CC0许可。

你的读者想找一份可使用的素材做小作品，不是研究这个机构全部历史。你准备把已经查过的内容整理成一页。

## 先猜一下

这一页需要让读者完成什么动作，哪些数字与背景可以不占开头？

先写下你的判断，再往下看答案。

## 答案

先说明能找到哪类材料、从哪里进入、选中素材后还要核对什么。数字可以帮助了解范围，但不必压过读者真正需要的下一步。

## 先写三块：用途、入口、检查

写下你自己的三块内容：想做什么作品；到哪个真实入口找对应材料；选中以后怎样确认出处、使用说明与是否含第三方内容。再决定是否需要补一条带查看日期的规模说明。

不要把这页写成“所有素材都已替你检查”。你完成的是清楚的导览，不是对每一件素材的全量许可审查。

:::detail[为什么不把两份页面所有数字都保留下来？]
读者现在要找到材料并开始制作，机构背景里的图书册数或档案体积未必用得上。保留当前需要的入口和检查方法，反而让一页更容易用。被省略的数据没有变成错误，只是不在这份成品的范围里。你可以在来源区保留完整入口，读者需要背景时再展开。[W3C的写作提示](https://www.w3.org/WAI/tips/writing/)强调清楚组织内容，在这里落实为每一块都对应读者要做的一步。
:::

根据读者改变的信息需求，决定继续编辑导览还是先寻找新的统计。

::play{#make-a-one-page-brief-weigh}

## 什么时候该反过来

读者改成研究资料使用人数时，现有导览就不能直接回答。此时需要取得定义与时期明确的使用统计，不能把原来的素材规模换个列名当作答案。

:::detail[同一页可以同时服务创作者和研究者吗？]
可以分成清楚的入口，但不要假装同一套数据已经解决两个不同问题。创作者需要找到素材及使用条件；研究者可能需要下载、浏览或独立用户的定义和统计周期。你可以在页尾说明另一个问题还需哪些材料，并指向尚待核对的统计入口。这样既保留了已经完成的导览，又没有把它包装成一份不存在的使用效果报告。范围明确，比标题写得无所不包更容易兑现。
:::

:::detail[做完这一页后，怎样实际验收？]
请自己按照页上的顺序走一遍：能否到真实入口，知道要找的材料类型，并说出选中以后需检查的项目？打开目标页时如果需要注册或网络不可用，要如实标出这一步，而不是把没有访问到的内容写成已确认。你可以让AI帮助调整导览的文字，但这几步实际检查仍需要真实动作。最后把已验证的入口与尚待确认的部分区分开，让下一个人不会把你的草稿当成全量审计。
:::

## 自检

不看原来的长笔记，只看你这一页。你能否指出一项可立即执行的动作、一条对应来源，以及一个没有替读者确认的边界？

## 一句话

**好简报让人迈出有依据的下一步，而不是把所有资料压成一页。**

en.title: Given Only One Page, What Information Would You Keep?
en.content:
# Given Only One Page, What Information Would You Keep?

## For People Looking to Create Something, a One-Page Brief Is Enough to Start

The [Smithsonian project page](https://www.si.edu/openaccess) provides search for open-access materials, 3D content, and access points for learning resources; the [dataset entry](https://registry.opendata.aws/smithsonian-open-access/) explains the open data and its CC0 license.

Your reader wants to find usable material to make a small project, not study the institution's entire history. You are preparing to organize what you have already looked up into a single page.

## Predict first
What action does this page need to enable the reader to take, and which figures and background details do not need to take up the beginning?

Write down your judgment first before looking at the answer below.

## Answer
First explain what types of material can be found, where to enter, and what still needs to be checked after selecting an asset. Numbers can help convey the scope, but they do not need to overshadow the next step the reader actually needs.

## Write Three Blocks First: Purpose, Access, and Checks

Write down your own three blocks: what project you want to create; which actual access point to use for finding the corresponding material; and how to confirm the source, usage instructions, and whether there is third-party content once an asset is selected. Then decide whether you need to add a note on collection scale with the date accessed.

Do not write this page as if "all materials have been checked for you." What you are delivering is a clear reference guide, not a full license audit for every single item.

:::detail[Why not keep all the numbers from both pages?]
The reader now needs to find materials and start creating; figures in the institutional background, such as book counts or archive volume, may not be useful right now. Keeping only the currently needed entry points and checking methods actually makes the single page easier to use. The omitted data has not become incorrect; it simply falls outside the scope of this deliverable. You can keep the complete access points in a sources section, allowing readers to expand them when they need background context. The [W3C writing tips](https://www.w3.org/WAI/tips/writing/) emphasize organizing content clearly, which here translates to making every block correspond to a step the reader needs to take.
:::

Based on the reader's changing information needs, decide whether to continue editing the guide or search for new statistics first.

::play{#make-a-one-page-brief-weigh}

## When to choose the other way

When the reader switches to studying how many people use the materials, the existing guide cannot answer that directly. At this point, you need usage statistics with clear definitions and time periods, rather than merely renaming a column for collection size to serve as the answer.

:::detail[Can the same page serve both creators and researchers?]
It can be divided into clear access points, but do not pretend that the same set of data has solved two different problems. Creators need to find materials and usage terms; researchers may need definitions and tracking periods for downloads, pageviews, or unique users. You can explain at the bottom of the page what additional materials the other question requires, and point to statistical access points that still need to be checked. This preserves the guide you have already completed without packaging it as a nonexistent usage-impact report. A clearly defined scope is much easier to deliver on than an all-inclusive title.
:::

:::detail[After completing this page, how do you actually verify it?]
Walk through the steps yourself in the order presented on the page: can you reach the actual access point, identify the type of material you are looking for, and state what items need checking once an asset is selected? If opening the destination page requires registration or the network is unavailable, record that step truthfully instead of marking content you never accessed as confirmed. You can ask an AI to help refine the guide's wording, but these practical verification steps still require real action. Finally, distinguish verified access points from parts still awaiting confirmation, so the next person will not mistake your draft for a full audit.
:::

## Check yourself
Without looking at your original long notes, look only at this single page. Can you point out one immediately actionable step, one corresponding source, and one boundary that has not been confirmed for the reader?

## In one sentence
**A good brief helps people take a well-grounded next step, rather than squeezing all information onto a single page.**
