lessons.title: 看不懂时，要更长的解释还是更小的一步？
lessons.content:
# 看不懂时，要更长的解释还是更小的一步？

## 词大致看懂了，动作却连不起来

[《爱丽丝漫游奇境》第一章](https://www.gutenberg.org/files/11/11-h/11-h.htm)的真实原文，把白兔说话、掏表、赶路与爱丽丝起身追去写在一个长段落里。这个故事是小说，不是现实新闻；本课的中文说明是自己的释义，不要求你已经会读英文。

你知道主要人物是谁，却分不清哪一个动作让爱丽丝改变了行动，准备请AI帮助理解。

## 先猜一下

你会怎样说出卡点，避免只得到一篇更长的整章介绍？

先写下你的判断，再往下看答案。

## 答案

指出已经理解的部分，再请它解释卡住的动作关系。可以让助手先标出转折前后各发生什么，把最后的判断留给你完成。

## 把“看不懂”缩成一个可以处理的问题

试着写：“我知道Alice是爱丽丝，Rabbit是白兔；请把这段里的动作分开，指出转折的位置，先不要替我解释她为什么追去。”

[AERO的明确教学指南](https://www.edresearch.edu.au/guides-resources/practice-guides/explicit-instruction-practice-guide-full-publication)讨论样例与引导练习。这里把帮助限制到一项动作，是为了让你还有可以亲手完成的下一步。

:::detail[我连人物是谁都不知道，还要先找转折吗？]
不用硬跳到后面的判断。先请它说明一个句子里谁做了什么，再自己试另一个句子。帮助应该落在你当前能接上的地方，而不是因为这门课安排了某个难度，就要求你假装已经理解前置内容。你可以保留自己的进度，同时查看更具体的提示；这不代表系统给你贴上了一个能力等级。把卡点说明白，让你自己选择需要的帮助，比笼统地要求所有解释都更简单更有效。
:::

先按自己的实际卡点选择帮助，不用把所有问题都变成整章重讲。

::play{#ask-for-the-step-you-missed-weigh}

## 什么时候该反过来

你想了解整章故事大概讲什么，整体介绍就可能合适。但要解决某一处动作关系，先处理那一处，不必重新从作者生平讲起。

:::detail[怎样检查助手真的回答了这次卡点？]
把你的请求与回复并排看。你问的是谁在什么时候起身，回复却讲了故事寓意，即使内容有趣，也没有完成当前动作。可以进一步说：“先回到这一段，标出动作与人物。”得到说明后，用原文或本课释义核对，不把助手的自信语气当作来源。你不是要求它永远只能回答一个句子，而是在明确这一轮先解决什么，之后再看要不要展开其他话题。
:::

:::detail[我该把原文提供多少给助手？]
提供足以判断当前关系的短段落即可，同时写清材料出自哪里。只给一句被截掉前因的文字，可能让它靠猜补关系；一次塞进整本书，又容易让讨论偏离你的问题。这里以白兔出现到爱丽丝追去的一段为范围，正好包含前后动作。若问题涉及下一段，再补入那一段并更新范围。你练的是选择能回答问题的材料，不是尽可能上传更多文字。如果回复谈到了原段没有出现的后来情节，就要求先回到已提供的范围。多知道一些故事，并不自动解决这一句的关系。
:::

## 自检

同一段中每个动作都能读懂，但你无法指出哪个在前哪个在后。你会怎样用一句话告诉助手这次的请求？

## 一句话

**先说明自己卡在哪一步，帮助才容易落到能继续做的地方。**

en.title: When You Do Not Understand, Do You Need a Longer Explanation or a Smaller Step?
en.content:
# When You Do Not Understand, Do You Need a Longer Explanation or a Smaller Step?

## You Roughly Understand the Words, but the Actions Do Not Connect

The actual original text of [Chapter 1 of Alice's Adventures in Wonderland](https://www.gutenberg.org/files/11/11-h/11-h.htm) puts the White Rabbit speaking, taking out a watch, hurrying away, and Alice getting up to chase after it all in one long paragraph. This story is fiction, not real-world news; the Chinese explanations in this lesson are its own paraphrases, and do not require that you already know how to read English.

You know who the main characters are, but you cannot tell which action made Alice change what she was doing, so you prepare to ask an AI for help understanding it.

## Predict first
How would you describe your sticking point so that you avoid simply receiving a longer introduction to the entire chapter?

Write down your assessment first, then scroll down to see the answer.

## Answer
Point out what you already understand, and then ask it to explain the relationship between the actions where you are stuck. You can have the assistant first mark what happens before and after the turning point, leaving the final judgment for you to complete.

## Shrink "Not Understanding" into a Manageable Problem

Try writing: "I know Alice is Alice and Rabbit is the White Rabbit; please separate the actions in this passage and point out the location of the turning point, without explaining for me yet why she chased after it."

[AERO's Explicit Instruction Practice Guide](https://www.edresearch.edu.au/guides-resources/practice-guides/explicit-instruction-practice-guide-full-publication) discusses worked examples and guided practice. Here, limiting the help to a single action is meant to leave you with a next step that you can complete yourself.

:::detail[If I do not even know who the characters are, do I still need to look for the turning point first?]
You do not have to force yourself to jump to subsequent judgments. First, ask it to explain who did what in one sentence, and then try another sentence yourself. Help should land where you can currently pick it up, rather than requiring you to pretend you already understand the prerequisite content just because this course set a certain level of difficulty. You can maintain your own pace while viewing more specific hints; this does not mean the system has labeled you with an ability level. Stating your sticking point clearly so that you can choose the help you need is simpler and more effective than vaguely asking for all explanations to be simpler.
:::

Choose help based on your actual sticking point first, without turning every question into a retelling of the entire chapter.

::play{#ask-for-the-step-you-missed-weigh}

## When to choose the other way

If you want to understand roughly what the entire chapter is about, an overall introduction may be appropriate. But to resolve a relationship between actions in a specific spot, handle that spot first without starting all over again from the author's biography.

:::detail[How do I check whether the assistant actually answered this sticking point?]
Look at your request and the response side by side. If you asked who got up and when, but the response discussed the moral of the story, then even if the content is interesting, it did not complete the current step. You can follow up by saying: "Let's go back to this paragraph first and mark the actions and characters." Once you receive the explanation, verify it against the original text or this lesson's paraphrase, rather than taking the assistant's confident tone as a factual source. You are not requiring it to only ever answer with a single sentence; you are clarifying what to resolve in this round first, and then deciding whether to expand into other topics afterward.
:::

:::detail[How much of the original text should I provide to the assistant?]
Providing a short paragraph sufficient to judge the current relationship is enough, while clearly stating where the material comes from. Providing only a single sentence with its preceding context cut off may cause the assistant to guess the relationship; stuffing in an entire book at once makes it easy for the discussion to drift away from your question. Here, the passage from the White Rabbit appearing to Alice chasing after it serves as the scope, which happens to include the actions before and after. If a question touches on the next paragraph, add that paragraph and update the scope. What you are practicing is selecting material that can answer your question, not uploading as much text as possible. If the response touches on later plot points that do not appear in the provided excerpt, ask it to return to the provided scope first. Knowing more of the story does not automatically resolve the relationship in this sentence.
:::

## Check yourself
You can understand every action in the same paragraph, but you cannot point out which comes first and which comes later. How would you state your request to the assistant in one sentence?

## In one sentence
**State which step you are stuck on first, so that help can easily land where you can keep going.**

lessons.title: 为什么要先写自己的判断，再看解释？
lessons.content:
# 为什么要先写自己的判断，再看解释？

## 先保留你还没看解释时的想法

[Khanmigo在2023年的试点介绍](https://blog.khanacademy.org/harnessing-ai-so-that-all-students-benefit-a-nonprofit-approach-for-equal-access/)展示了先提问、给提示的辅导设计。现在用一份能够直接核对的文学材料试试这个顺序。

在[爱丽丝开篇](https://www.gutenberg.org/files/11/11-h/11-h.htm)的长段里，白兔先说自己要迟到，后来从背心口袋拿出表。先不看下面的解释，你准备判断是哪一步让爱丽丝站起来。

## 先猜一下

你会先记下什么，才能在看完解释后发现自己原来具体想错或不确定在哪里？

先写下你的判断，再往下看答案。

## 答案

先写自己的判断，以及用来支持它的那一点线索。解释出现后，比较线索是否对应原文，比只说“这个答案看着对”更清楚。

## 先留一小段自己的证据

可以先写“我认为是在……，因为这句话……”；不确定就写明不确定。然后回到原文：作者用转折把听见说话与看见掏表分开，后面才描写爱丽丝起身追去。

你现在能看出自己是只凭“会说话很奇怪”做判断，还是找到了叙述中的动作位置。

:::detail[猜错了，会不会把错误记得更牢？]
本课的做法不是让错误无人纠正地重复，而是先留下当前理解，再及时对照材料查出差异。要是发现自己选了白兔说话，就回到原文看作者怎么写当时的反应与后来的起身。重点是为下一次阅读改进检查方法，而不是给一次猜测贴标签。Khanmigo的试点设计提供了提问与提示的思路，但没有证明你只做这一题就必然获得长期效果；这里仍需要后面的独立尝试与复习。
:::

:::detail[完全不知道时，是不是也要随便猜一个？]
可以写“我不确定，因为没分清这一句的行动者”，它同样暴露了一个可处理的卡点。你不必为了留下答案而装作有把握。随后先找适量帮助，再独立完成一个接得上的动作。低压力的预测不是让所有人必须抢答，而是给自己的初始状态留一个真实记录。若已经看过完整解释，这一轮就记录为看后练习，换一个尚未讲过的位置再观察独立判断。
:::

:::detail[为什么要写理由，而不仅是一个词？]
同一个正确选项可能来自不同过程：你可能找到了原句，也可能只是碰巧选中了。留一小句理由，有助于发现依据是否真的支持答案。这里不要求长论文，只要指出转折、动作或某个词的位置。AI给出反馈后，你仍能用这句记录追问具体问题，而不是只能说“我不懂为什么不对”。理由服务于检查与继续学习，不是为了让每一个小练习都变得沉重。
:::

这些是学习过程的记录样式，不是真实受试者成绩。区分哪些还保留着解释出现前的独立判断。

::play{#predict-before-the-answer-sort}

## 自检

你已经熟悉白兔掏表这一段。下一次如何换一个尚未讲解的位置，避免把记住原题当成新的独立判断？

## 一句话

**先留自己的判断与依据，再看解释，才能看见需要改变的那一步。**

en.title: Why Write Down Your Judgment Before Reading the Explanation?
en.content:
# Why Write Down Your Judgment Before Reading the Explanation?

## Preserve your thinking before reading the explanation

[Khanmigo's 2023 pilot introduction](https://blog.khanacademy.org/harnessing-ai-so-that-all-students-benefit-a-nonprofit-approach-for-equal-access/) demonstrated a tutoring design that asks questions and offers hints first. Now try this sequence using a piece of literature that you can check directly.

In the long opening passage of [Alice](https://www.gutenberg.org/files/11/11-h/11-h.htm), the White Rabbit first says he is going to be late, and later takes a watch out of his waistcoat pocket. Without looking at the explanation below, prepare to judge which step makes Alice stand up.

## Predict first
What would you jot down first so that, after reading the explanation, you can see specifically where you were mistaken or uncertain?

Write down your judgment first, then read on for the answer.

## Answer
Write down your own judgment first, along with the specific clue you used to support it. Once the explanation appears, comparing whether that clue corresponds to the original text is much clearer than simply saying, "this answer looks right."

## Record a brief piece of your own evidence first

You can start by writing, "I think it was when..., because this sentence says..."; if you are not sure, state clearly that you are uncertain. Then return to the original text: the author uses a shift to separate hearing the rabbit speak from seeing him take out the watch, and only then describes Alice getting up to chase after him.

You can now see whether you made your judgment solely based on "a talking rabbit is weird," or if you actually located the action in the narrative.

:::detail[If you guess wrong, will you remember the mistake more firmly?]
The approach in this lesson is not to let mistakes repeat uncorrected, but to capture your current understanding first and then promptly check the material to spot discrepancies. If you find that you chose the White Rabbit speaking, return to the original text to see how the author wrote her reaction at that moment versus her getting up later. The point is to improve your checking method for the next reading, rather than labeling a single guess. Khanmigo's pilot design provided the concept of questions and hints, but it did not prove that doing this single question guarantees long-term results; independent practice and review are still needed afterward.
:::

:::detail[If you have no idea at all, should you just make a random guess?]
You can write, "I am not sure, because I could not tell who was acting in this sentence," which likewise reveals an actionable sticking point. You do not have to pretend to be confident just to put down an answer. Next, seek a moderate amount of help, and then independently complete a coherent follow-up step. Low-stakes prediction is not about forcing everyone to buzz in quickly; it is about leaving an honest record of your initial state. If you have already seen the full explanation, record this round as practice after reading, and choose another unanalyzed spot to observe your independent judgment.
:::

:::detail[Why write a reason instead of just a single word?]
The same correct option can come from different processes: you might have found the original sentence, or you might have simply picked it by chance. Leaving a brief reason helps you see whether your evidence actually supports the answer. A long essay is not required here—just point out where a transition, an action, or a particular word occurs. After the AI gives feedback, you can still use this recorded note to ask specific follow-up questions, instead of only being able to say, "I don't understand why it's wrong." Reasons serve verification and ongoing learning; they are not meant to make every small exercise burdensome.
:::

These are sample records from the learning process, not actual test-subject scores. Distinguish which ones still preserve independent judgment before the explanation appeared.

::play{#predict-before-the-answer-sort}

## Check yourself
You are already familiar with the passage where the White Rabbit pulls out the watch. Next time, how can you switch to an unanalyzed spot to avoid mistaking your memory of the original question for new independent judgment?

## In one sentence
**Keep your own judgment and evidence before reading the explanation, so you can see the step that needs to change.**

lessons.title: 一条提示，怎样既帮忙又不替你做完？
lessons.content:
# 一条提示，怎样既帮忙又不替你做完？

## 两种帮助，留下的下一步不同

你要读懂[爱丽丝开篇的动作变化](https://www.gutenberg.org/files/11/11-h/11-h.htm)。有人准备直接给出整段动作顺序，也有人准备先示范一句，再请你检查后面的转折。

[AERO指南](https://www.edresearch.edu.au/guides-resources/practice-guides/explicit-instruction-practice-guide-full-publication)讨论样例和逐步减少指导，[Khanmigo试点](https://blog.khanacademy.org/harnessing-ai-so-that-all-students-benefit-a-nonprofit-approach-for-equal-access/)展示了提问式帮助。下面的帮助安排是本课设计，不是对真实模型的一次测量。

## 先猜一下

怎样判断这一轮该看多少示范，才能既接得上，又还留有自己完成的部分？

先写下你的判断，再往下看答案。

## 答案

先看是否理解完成任务所需的基本动作。基础还没有时看一个示范；能够继续时，把提示停在方向或位置，把下一项判断留给自己。

## 提示指路，示范展示怎样走

第一次认不出行动者，可以看一句示范：先找人物，再找它做的动作。已经会这一项后，提示可以缩成“看看转折前后各是谁在行动”。

两者都可以有用。区别在于你这次还需要哪一项帮助，以及帮助以后还剩哪一项实际练习。

:::detail[提示越少，是不是学习就一定越好？]
不能这样判断。过少的帮助可能让你连任务要求都无法理解，最后只是在猜按钮。这里不追求一种永远最少的提示，而是让你能够完成当前可掌握的步骤。你可以主动展开示范，也可以在会做时选择自己试。课程不会因为你用了提示就自动判断你能力低，也不应因为连续答对就悄悄提升难度。保留学习者的选择，同时用新的尝试查看方法是否真的能用。
:::

比较两个明确的辅导规则：总给完整过程，或按当前卡点提供恰当帮助。这里只比较提供的内容，不推断学习成绩。

::play{#use-a-hint-not-a-finished-answer-contrast}

## 完成以后，检查留下了哪一种能力

问自己：没有这段完整答案，我还能在另一句里找出人物、动作与转折吗？能指出依据，比重复刚才的整段话更接近本次目标。

:::detail[完整示范与代写答案，为什么有时看起来一样？]
文字本身可能一样，区别来自它在学习中的位置。第一次展示一个样例，是为了让你看懂步骤；把这份样例直接当成你已经独立完成的作业，就混淆了两件事。可以明确标记“这是示范”，接着换一句让你试。你也可以把AI生成的完整分析当作对照材料，但不要据此给自己记录未发生的独立完成。保留这种身份区别，才能诚实观察哪些部分仍需要帮助。
:::

:::detail[怎样向助手要求一条不泄题的提示？]
说明提示只指出检查方向，并点名不要交出的部分。例如“告诉我应该注意哪一种连接词，先不要列出整段动作顺序”。收到后看看它是否真的只给了方向；若已经把全部答案说出，这一轮就视作示范，另找短句练习，不用假装答案没有出现。这样的请求不是保证模型一定遵守，而是让你拥有一个能检查帮助边界的条件。需要完整说明时，也可以主动改成示范请求。
:::

:::detail[这次练习留下的“收据”是什么？]
保留你在提示以后亲自做的那一项：自己选中的位置、解释的一小句，以及回到原文核对后的修正。它不必是正式成绩，也不需要保存整段对话。提示已经把答案给出时，收据就应说明这是看后练习；只指路以后由你完成时，则记录用了哪类帮助。这样下次继续学，才知道哪些动作是自己做的，不会因为屏幕上已经有一份完整结果，就把所有步骤都算在自己名下。
:::

## 自检

你要求一条提示，回复却给出了完整答案。下一步怎样记录这一轮，并安排一次真正独立的新尝试？

## 一句话

**帮助的分量看当前卡点；示范结束后，还要有自己能接着做的一步。**

en.title: How Can a Hint Help Without Doing the Work for You?
en.content:
# How Can a Hint Help Without Doing the Work for You?

## Two Types of Help, Leaving Different Next Steps

You want to understand [how Alice's actions change in the opening scene](https://www.gutenberg.org/files/11/11-h/11-h.htm). One person is ready to give you the entire sequence of actions directly, while another plans to demonstrate one sentence first, then ask you to check the subsequent turning point.

[The AERO Guide](https://www.edresearch.edu.au/guides-resources/practice-guides/explicit-instruction-practice-guide-full-publication) discusses worked examples and fading guidance, while [the Khanmigo pilot](https://blog.khanacademy.org/harnessing-ai-so-that-all-students-benefit-a-nonprofit-approach-for-equal-access/) demonstrates inquiry-based help. The arrangement of help below is an instructional design for this lesson, not a measurement of a real model.

## Predict first
How do you determine how much demonstration to view in this round so that you can follow along while still leaving a part to complete on your own?

Write down your judgment first, then scroll down to read the answer.

## Answer
First check whether you understand the basic actions needed to complete the task. When you do not yet have the basics, look at one demonstration; once you can keep going, stop the hint at pointing out a direction or location, and leave the next judgment to yourself.

## Hints Point the Way, Demonstrations Show How to Walk It

If you cannot identify the actor the first time, you can view a one-sentence demonstration: find the character first, then find the action they perform. Once you already know how to do this, the hint can be shortened to "Look at who is acting before and after the turning point."

Both can be useful. The difference lies in which specific help you still need this time, and which practical exercise remains after the help.

:::detail[Does fewer hints necessarily mean better learning?]
You cannot make that judgment. Too little help might leave you unable even to understand the task requirements, ending up just guessing which button to click. The goal here is not to pursue a hint that is always as minimal as possible, but rather to enable you to complete the steps you can currently master. You can choose to expand a demonstration, or you can choose to try on your own when you know how. The course does not automatically judge you as low-ability simply because you used a hint, nor should it quietly increase the difficulty just because you answered correctly several times in a row. Preserve the learner's choice, while using a new attempt to see whether the method truly works.
:::

Compare two explicit tutoring rules: always providing the full process, or offering appropriate help based on the current sticking point. This comparison looks only at the content provided and does not infer learning outcomes.

::play{#use-a-hint-not-a-finished-answer-contrast}

## After Finishing, Check What Ability Remains

Ask yourself: without this complete answer, could I still find the character, action, and turning point in another sentence? Being able to point to the evidence brings you closer to this lesson's goal than simply repeating the entire passage from earlier.

:::detail[Why do a full demonstration and an answer written for you sometimes look identical?]
The text itself may look the same; the difference comes from its place in the learning process. Presenting a worked example for the first time is meant to help you understand the steps; taking that example directly as an assignment you completed independently confuses the two things. You can clearly mark it as "This is a demonstration," and then switch to another sentence for you to try. You can also use an AI-generated full analysis as reference material for comparison, but do not use it to credit yourself with an independent completion that never took place. Preserving this distinction in identity allows you to honestly observe which parts still require help.
:::

:::detail[How do you ask an assistant for a hint that does not give away the answer?]
Specify that the hint should only point out a direction to check, and explicitly name the parts not to hand over. For example: "Tell me which type of connective I should pay attention to, but do not list the full sequence of actions yet." Once you receive the response, see whether it truly only gave a direction; if it already revealed the entire answer, treat this round as a demonstration and find another short sentence to practice with, without pretending the answer never appeared. Making such a request does not guarantee that the model will follow it, but it gives you a condition to check the boundaries of the help. When you need a full explanation, you can also take the initiative to change it to a demonstration request.
:::

:::detail[What is the "receipt" left behind by this practice?]
Keep the specific step you performed yourself after receiving the hint: the position you selected on your own, the brief explanatory sentence you wrote, and the correction you made after checking back against the original text. It does not have to be a formal grade, nor does it require saving the entire conversation. When the hint has already given away the answer, the receipt should indicate that this was practice done after viewing the answer; when it only pointed the way and you completed the work, record which type of help was used. That way, when you continue studying next time, you will know which actions were your own work, rather than crediting yourself with every step simply because a complete result was displayed on the screen.
:::

## Check yourself
You requested a hint, but the response provided the full answer. How should you record this round for your next step, and how should you arrange a truly independent new attempt?

## In one sentence
**The amount of help depends on your current sticking point; after a demonstration ends, there must still be a step you can continue doing on your own.**

lessons.title: 换成自己的话，怎样检查有没有走样？
lessons.content:
# 换成自己的话，怎样检查有没有走样？

## 换成自己的话，意思还在吗？

你已经读过[爱丽丝开篇](https://www.gutenberg.org/files/11/11-h/11-h.htm)：作者把听见白兔说话，与看到它从背心口袋拿表分开叙述。现在合上现成的中文解释，用自己的话说明爱丽丝为什么开始追去。

[AERO的法语课堂实例](https://www.edresearch.edu.au/guides-resources/practice-resources/spacing-and-retrieval-example-practice)展示了把已学词语重新取用并组合的做法。本课借此安排重新表达，不把课堂案例冒充这里的学习效果实验。

## 先猜一下

怎样判断自己的说法只是换了措辞，还是把原文的关系也改掉了？

先写下你的判断，再往下看答案。

## 答案

回到原段检查人物、动作与转折是否对应。表达可以不同，但不能把作者区分开的两个反应合成同一个原因。

## 先说一遍，再对照一处关键关系

写两句自己的解释，不必使用“转折”这种术语。随后打开原段，指出哪一处支持起身追去的原因，哪一处说明此前的反应。

如果你的话写成“一听白兔说话，她立即追去”，就回看作者为何在后面又写了掏表与起身。修的是关系，不是某个漂亮词。

:::detail[不用和讲解一样的词，会不会被判成不懂？]
理解检查应该围绕这次要掌握的关系，而不是要求照搬老师的风格。你可以写“那只兔子拿出表，这才让她好奇地跟了上去”，也可以用另一种短表达；关键是能够指回原文，并保留说话时与掏表时反应的区别。正式练习的短答案用于核对一个有限判断，不代表你的全部解释必须只包含那个短语。遇到不同说法时，应检查含义与依据，而不是用字面长度代替理解。
:::

:::detail[只靠记得情节，为什么还要找支持位置？]
记忆可能混入故事梗概、电影画面或后面才出现的情节。本次任务只检查选定的原段，因此要能指出依据在哪里。找回位置会暴露你是否把“我熟悉这个故事”误当成“这一段确实这样写”。你可以先凭记忆解释，再打开材料核对；两步分别有用。若发现记错，保留是哪一个关系改了，而不必把自己贴成不会阅读的人。下一次再换一处关系练习即可。
:::

:::detail[怎样用AI帮助检查自己的解释，而不是让它代写？]
把自己的两句话与所用原段一起提供，要求它指出一处可能不对应的位置，不要直接替你重写全文。得到建议后，你亲自回去核对并修改。要是它提到原段之外的情节，就要求回到限定的材料。这样AI是帮助定位问题的工具，决定是否修改仍有明确依据。没有AI也能做这个检查：自己把解释中的每个动作划出来，逐个找对应位置。
:::

判断这些原创释义是否保持了所选原段的关系。它们不是已有译本的引文。

::play{#explain-it-back-sort}

## 自检

你的解释读起来通顺，却无法找到支持其中一个动作的句子。应先删掉、补查，还是让语气更肯定？你会怎样决定？

## 一句话

**用自己的话解释，再用原材料核对关系，理解才不只是一段熟悉文字。**

en.title: When Putting It in Your Own Words, How Do You Check That Meaning Hasn't Drifted?
en.content:
# When Putting It in Your Own Words, How Do You Check That Meaning Hasn't Drifted?

## When you put it into your own words, is the meaning still there?

You have already read [the opening of Alice](https://www.gutenberg.org/files/11/11-h/11-h.htm): the author recounts hearing the White Rabbit speak separately from seeing it take a watch out of its waistcoat-pocket. Now close ready-made Chinese explanations and explain in your own words why Alice began chasing after it.

[AERO's French classroom example](https://www.edresearch.edu.au/guides-resources/practice-resources/spacing-and-retrieval-example-practice) illustrates the practice of retrieving and recombining previously learned words. This lesson draws on this to frame re-expression, without misrepresenting a classroom case study as an experiment on learning outcomes here.

## Predict first
How do you tell whether your explanation merely changed the wording, or also altered the relationships in the original text?

Write down your judgment first before looking at the answer below.

## Answer
Return to the original passage to check whether the characters, actions, and turning points match. The wording can be different, but you must not combine the two reactions that the author kept separate into a single cause.

## Explain it once first, then check one key relationship

Write two sentences of your own explanation without needing to use technical terms like "turning point." Then open the original passage and point out which part supports the reason for getting up and chasing after it, and which part describes the earlier reaction.

If your wording is "as soon as she heard the White Rabbit speak, she ran after it immediately," look back at why the author later wrote about taking out the watch and getting up. What you are revising is the relationship, not a pretty word.

:::detail[If I don't use the same words as the explanation, will it be judged as not understanding?]
Checking understanding should focus on the relationships to be mastered this time, rather than requiring you to copy the teacher's style. You could write "the rabbit took out a watch, and only then did she curiously follow," or use another short phrasing; the key is being able to point back to the original text and preserve the distinction between the reaction when it spoke and the reaction when it took out the watch. Short answers in formal exercises are used to verify a limited judgment; they do not mean your entire explanation must contain only that phrase. When encountering different phrasings, check meaning and evidence rather than substituting literal length for understanding.
:::

:::detail[Why do I still need to find supporting citations if I already remember the plot?]
Memory can mix in plot summaries, movie scenes, or plot developments that appear only later. This task only checks the selected original passage, so you must be able to point out where the evidence lies. Locating the exact spot reveals whether you mistook "I am familiar with this story" for "this passage is indeed written this way." You can explain from memory first and then open the material to check; both steps are useful in their own right. If you find you misremembered, note which relationship was changed, without needing to label yourself as someone who cannot read. You can simply practice with another relationship next time.
:::

:::detail[How can I use AI to help check my explanation instead of having it write for me?]
Provide your two sentences together with the original passage used, and ask it to point out one place that might not correspond, rather than having it directly rewrite the entire text for you. After receiving suggestions, go back yourself to verify and revise. If it mentions plot details outside the original passage, ask it to return to the bounded material. In this way, AI is a tool to help locate problems, while decisions about whether to revise still rest on clear evidence. You can also do this check without AI: underline each action in your explanation yourself and locate the corresponding place one by one.
:::

Determine whether these original paraphrases preserve the relationships in the selected original passage. They are not quotations from existing translations.

::play{#explain-it-back-sort}

## Check yourself
Your explanation reads smoothly, yet you cannot find a sentence supporting one of the actions. Should you delete it first, check further, or make your tone more confident? How would you decide?

## In one sentence
**Explain in your own words, then check relationships against the source material; only then is understanding more than just familiar text.**

lessons.title: 今天答对了，复习为什么还要留到以后？
lessons.content:
# 今天答对了，复习为什么还要留到以后？

## 刚看过与隔一段时间再想，是两次不同的检查

[AERO的法语课堂实践](https://www.edresearch.edu.au/guides-resources/practice-resources/spacing-and-retrieval-example-practice)把新词分组，并在后来回顾旧词、通过低压力小测重新取用它们。

现在换一份短小的非虚构材料：[NASA在2023年10月16日发布的观月夜公告](https://www.nasa.gov/news-release/celebrate-international-observe-the-moon-night-at-nasas-goddard-space-flight-center/)宣布当年10月21日的活动。你刚分清消息发布与活动举行是两个动作，准备安排下一次练习。

## 先猜一下

你会怎样安排下一次，才能看到离开解释以后还留下了哪些理解？

先写下你的判断，再往下看答案。

## 答案

隔一段时间先尝试回忆或重新判断，再打开材料核对。刚看后的顺畅与后来还能自己完成，是两种不同记录。

## 下次先做一小步，再看材料

下次先写下自己记得的两个日期分别对应什么，并说明哪里不确定，再回到公告核对。也可以换一份公告，先分清它的消息日与活动日。

这不是要求你在固定第几小时必须复习。先安排一次能实际执行的回访，再根据自己的真实作答调整。

:::detail[为什么不连续多读几遍就结束？]
重读可以帮助刚开始理解文字，但答案一直在眼前时，你不容易知道自己离开它以后还能做多少。把某一次检查放到稍后，先尝试再打开，就能区分熟悉感与重新取用的表现。这里不声称某个间隔适合所有人，也不把这份日期练习等同于AERO课堂中的全部做法。你需要的是一条可以观察的学习记录：这一次自己说出了什么，哪一处还要靠提示。
:::

按现在的状态选择下一步，不把刚开始理解与稍后检验混在一起。

::play{#return-to-it-later-weigh}

## 什么时候该反过来

刚开始就没看懂时，先把那个基础步骤弄清楚，不必急着延迟测试。延迟练习不是让你把无法理解的东西暂时搁置，然后责怪自己忘记。

:::detail[复习时忘了，是不是前面全白学了？]
一次忘记只说明这次没有顺利取用，不足以替你的全部学习下结论。先找回必要提示，重新完成那个动作，再记录需要补练的地方。不要为了保持连续答对，把提示后的完成改记成独立完成；也不要为了显得严格，把以前真正做过的部分全部抹掉。保留不同事实，就能安排更具体的下一步。学习记录的作用是帮助继续，而不是让你维护一张永远漂亮的成绩表。
:::

:::detail[以后回来，只检查记住几个数字够不够？]
要看你原来学的目标。如果目标是分清消息发布与活动举行，只记得10月21日还不够，得说清它对应哪个动作；如果目标是记住一组词，那么词义与用法就是另一种检查。复习应该重新触及原来的判断，而不只是随手问一个最容易记住的细节。你可以为下一次留下一个短问题，提醒自己做哪一种动作，不必把所有正文都复制到提醒里。再换一份公告检查日期身份，就能看见自己是否只记住了这一组数字。如果数字记得很准、日期身份却颠倒了，下一次先补练这层对应，而不只是继续背同一串数字。
:::

## 自检

几天后你能记起答案，却讲不清根据。下一次复习问题应该怎样写，才能提醒你补做找依据这一步？

## 一句话

**先弄懂，再隔一段时间自己试；两次表现分别记录。**

en.title: If You Got It Right Today, Why Save Review for Later?
en.content:
# If You Got It Right Today, Why Save Review for Later?

## Checking Right After and Recalling After a Pause Are Two Different Checks

[AERO's French classroom practice](https://www.edresearch.edu.au/guides-resources/practice-resources/spacing-and-retrieval-example-practice) groups new words, revisits old words later, and retrieves them through low-stakes quizzes.

Now switch to a short non-fiction text: [NASA's announcement released on October 16, 2023](https://www.nasa.gov/news-release/celebrate-international-observe-the-moon-night-at-nasas-goddard-space-flight-center/) announced an event on October 21 of that year. Having just distinguished between news release and event occurrence as two separate actions, you prepare to schedule the next practice.

## Predict first
How would you schedule the next session so that you can see what understanding remains once you step away from the explanation?

Write down your judgment first before looking at the answer below.

## Answer
After a pause, try recalling or judging again first before opening the material to check. Fluency right after reading and being able to complete it on your own later are two different records.

## Take a Small Step First Next Time Before Checking the Material

Next time, first write down what each of the two dates you remember corresponds to, note what you are unsure about, and then return to the announcement to check. You can also switch to another announcement and distinguish its news date from its event date first.

This is not asking you to review at a mandatory fixed hour. Schedule a follow-up that you can realistically carry out first, then adjust based on your actual responses.

:::detail[Why not just reread it several times in a row and call it done?]
Rereading can help with initial text comprehension, but when the answer is right in front of you, it is not easy to know how much you can do once you step away from it. Putting a check later and attempting it first before opening the text lets you distinguish a sense of familiarity from retrieval performance. This does not claim that a specific interval suits everyone, nor does it equate this date exercise with all practices in AERO classrooms. What you need is an observable learning record: what you stated on your own this time, and where you still had to rely on hints.
:::

Choose the next step based on your current state, without mixing initial understanding with later testing.

::play{#return-to-it-later-weigh}

## When to choose the other way

When you do not understand from the start, clarify that foundational step first rather than rushing into delayed testing. Delayed practice is not about shelving things you cannot understand and then blaming yourself for forgetting.

:::detail[If you forget during review, does it mean all previous learning was wasted?]
A single lapse of forgetting only indicates that retrieval was not smooth this time; it is not enough to pass judgment on all your learning. Retrieve the necessary hints first, complete that action again, and then record where additional practice is needed. Do not alter a hint-assisted completion to independent completion just to maintain a streak of correct answers; nor should you erase what you genuinely accomplished before just to appear rigorous. Preserving distinct facts allows you to arrange more concrete next steps. The purpose of a learning record is to help you continue, not to maintain a perpetually flawless report card.
:::

:::detail[When returning later, is it enough just to check whether you remember a few numbers?]
It depends on your original learning goal. If the goal was to distinguish between news release and event occurrence, merely remembering October 21 is not enough—you must articulate which action it corresponds to; if the goal was to memorize a set of words, word meaning and usage would be a different check. Review should re-engage the original judgment, not merely ask about whichever detail is easiest to memorize offhand. You can leave a short question for next time to remind yourself which action to take, without copying the entire text into the reminder. Switching to another announcement to check the role of the dates will reveal whether you only memorized this set of numbers. If the numbers are remembered accurately but the roles of the dates are reversed, practice this correspondence next time instead of simply continuing to memorize the same string of digits.
:::

## Check yourself
A few days later, you can recall the answer, but cannot explain the basis for it. How should the next review question be phrased to remind you to carry out the step of finding the evidence?

## In one sentence
**Understand it first, then try on your own after a pause; record the two performances separately.**

lessons.title: 一张小卡，能提醒你做哪一步？
lessons.content:
# 一张小卡，能提醒你做哪一步？

## 一张卡，是让你看答案，还是让你做判断？

你刚用[NASA的2023年观月夜公告](https://www.nasa.gov/news-release/celebrate-international-observe-the-moon-night-at-nasas-goddard-space-flight-center/)分清消息日与活动日，也看到[AERO的课堂实例](https://www.edresearch.edu.au/guides-resources/practice-resources/spacing-and-retrieval-example-practice)怎样把学过的内容重新取用。现在准备做一张自己的复习卡。

你可以把完整日期解释直接放在正面，也可以先放一个需要判断的问题，把依据留到翻面以后。

## 先猜一下

这张卡怎样安排，才能让你回来时知道要做哪一步，而不只是再看一次解释？

先写下你的判断，再往下看答案。

## 答案

正面写一个明确的判断问题，背面放短理由与对应来源。把问题限制在一个动作上，答案出现前才有自己的尝试。

## 给未来的自己留一项可执行动作

写一张自己的卡：正面问怎样区分公告里的消息日与活动日，背面写支持判断的动作词与原始入口。不要把问题与答案一起摆在正面。

读卡时先说出判断，再翻面检查。你可以使用University已有的复习与讲一遍功能，也可以先写在自己的笔记里。

:::detail[一张卡放很多问题，不是更省事吗？]
回来时你可能只答出了其中一半，却不知道这张卡该算哪种完成。把一个判断做清楚，更容易记录卡在哪里。例如判断日期身份是一张卡，辨认另一个生词可以另做一张。你不是要把长课拆成无数碎片，而是让每次复习都有明确对象。若两个小问题本来共同构成一个不可分的判断，可以放在一起，但要能说清怎样检查这一项，而不是凭整张卡看起来熟悉就翻过去。
:::

按照用途选择卡片结构：你需要复习一个判断，还是随手查一项步骤？

::play{#make-your-learning-card-weigh}

## 什么时候该反过来

你只需要随时查阅一份步骤清单时，可以做参考页，不必藏起内容让自己回忆。参考页帮助执行，复习卡帮助再次尝试，先选你现在需要哪一种。

:::detail[卡片背面为什么还值得留下来源？]
短答案可能随着重复变成一句失去背景的口号。保留对应原段或资料位置，让你忘记理由时可以重新查看，而不是光信卡片这么写。来源不必占据正面，也不需要复制全文；一个清楚的入口与位置提示就能帮助你回去核对。把卡分享给别人时，还应说明这是一张自己的学习卡，不是原作者给出的教学解释，避免把你的概括误当成正式注释。以后来源入口有变化时，这些标题与位置提示也方便重新查找，而不是只剩一张无法追溯来历的孤立卡片。
:::

:::detail[怎样检查卡片练的是方法，不只是记住原题？]
在适当的时候换一小段同样能找到日期与事件关系的公告，先用相同检查方法做，再核对。原卡可以保留，但不要把对熟题的快速回答当成所有材料都已掌握。你也可以在背面加一句“下次换段找依据”，提醒自己还有迁移练习。这里不要求每次都找新材料，而是让练习既有熟悉内容的回访，也有检验方法能否移用的机会。换材料时，保留判断问题的结构，不把旧公告的日期自动带进新卡。新答案也需要自己的来源位置。
:::

## 自检

读到另一份短材料，你能否自己写一个判断问题、一个有出处的理由，以及一条以后怎样重新检查的提示？

## 一句话

**复习卡安排一次判断，参考页支持一次执行；按用途选择。**

en.title: Which Step Can a Small Card Remind You to Take?
en.content:
# Which Step Can a Small Card Remind You to Take?

## Is a Card for Looking at the Answer, or for Making a Judgment?

You just used [NASA's 2023 Observe the Moon Night announcement](https://www.nasa.gov/news-release/celebrate-international-observe-the-moon-night-at-nasas-goddard-space-flight-center/) to distinguish the news release date from the event date, and also saw how [AERO's classroom example](https://www.edresearch.edu.au/guides-resources/practice-resources/spacing-and-retrieval-example-practice) retrieves previously learned content. Now you are getting ready to make a review card of your own.

You can put the full date explanation directly on the front, or you can first put a question that requires a judgment, leaving the evidence for after turning the card over.

## Predict first
How should this card be arranged so that when you come back, you know which step to take, rather than just looking at the explanation again?

Write down your judgment first, then look below for the answer.

## Answer
Write a clear judgment question on the front, and put a brief reason along with the corresponding source on the back. Limit the question to a single action so that you make your own attempt before the answer appears.

## Leave an Actionable Step for Your Future Self

Write a card of your own: ask on the front how to distinguish the news release date from the event date in the announcement, and write the action words supporting the judgment along with the original entry point on the back. Do not put both the question and the answer on the front.

When reading the card, state your judgment first, then flip it over to check. You can use University's existing review and explain-it-back features, or you can write it in your own notes first.

:::detail[Wouldn't it be easier to put many questions on one card?]
When you come back, you might only answer half of them, without knowing which kind of completion this card counts as. Making a single judgment clear makes it easier to record where you got stuck. For example, judging date roles is one card, and identifying another new word can be another card. You are not trying to break a long lesson into countless fragments, but rather ensuring that each review has a clear target. If two small questions originally form an indivisible judgment together, they can be placed together, but you must be able to state clearly how to check this item, rather than simply flipping over the card just because the whole card looks familiar.
:::

Choose a card structure based on its purpose: do you need to review a judgment, or conveniently look up a step?

::play{#make-your-learning-card-weigh}

## When to choose the other way

When you only need to consult a checklist of steps at any time, you can make a reference page without having to hide content to make yourself recall it. A reference page helps with execution, while a review card helps with trying again; first choose which one you need right now.

:::detail[Why is it still worth keeping the source on the back of the card?]
A short answer may turn into a slogan that has lost its context through repetition. Keeping the corresponding original paragraph or source location allows you to check again when you forget the reason, rather than simply believing what the card says. The source does not need to take up the front, nor does it require copying the full text; a clear entry point and location cue can help you go back and check. When sharing cards with others, you should also clarify that this is your own learning card, not an instructional explanation provided by the original author, avoiding having your summary mistaken for an official annotation. When source access points change in the future, these titles and location cues also make it convenient to look them up again, rather than leaving behind an isolated card whose origin cannot be traced.
:::

:::detail[How do you check that the card trains the method, not just memorizing the original question?]
At an appropriate time, switch to another short announcement where date-and-event relationships can also be found, apply the same checking method first, and then verify. You can keep the original card, but do not mistake a quick answer to a familiar question for having mastered all material. You can also add a line on the back, "Find evidence in a different passage next time," reminding yourself of transfer practice. This does not require finding new material every time; rather, it ensures practice has both revisits to familiar content and opportunities to test whether the method can be transferred. When switching materials, keep the structure of the judgment question without automatically bringing the dates from the old announcement into the new card. The new answer also requires its own source location.
:::

## Check yourself
When reading another short piece of material, can you write a judgment question, a sourced reason, and a reminder on how to recheck it in the future on your own?

## In one sentence
**A review card arranges a judgment, while a reference page supports execution; choose based on purpose.**

lessons.title: 先列一百个点子，还是先问在哪里做？
lessons.content:
# 先列一百个点子，还是先问在哪里做？

## 一份办活动的指南，先问你打算邀请谁

[NASA的观月夜主办指南](https://science.nasa.gov/moon/observe-the-moon-night/how-to-host/)提供了筹备一次观月活动的真实参考。你准备据此做一份任务单，还没定好这次活动的形式。

你没有举办活动或预订场地，现在的第一句请求只是：“帮我安排一个很棒的观月夜。”

## 先猜一下

在要求详细时间表之前，你会先补充哪些会改变整个方案的条件？

先写下你的判断，再往下看答案。

## 答案

先说明受众、活动形式、可用资源以及仍待确认的场地或平台。一个漂亮时间表不能替你决定这些前提，也不能把未确认条件写成已经安排好。

## 先让条件有名字，再让方案有细节

你可以请求：“先根据指南列出必须确认的条件，不填写我还没提供的人数、地点和负责人；等这些清楚以后，再安排任务顺序。”

这时AI帮你整理问题，而不是替你凭空建立一场已经获准的活动。

:::detail[没有确定人数，就完全不能开始吗？]
可以先做不依赖精确人数的工作，比如整理可选形式、列出需要确认的条件与相关来源。只是不要把尚未确定的数字写进对外承诺。草稿可以有待填写的栏位，也可以明确比较小型聚会与线上介绍需要哪些不同准备。你推进的是一项有范围的筹备工作，不是等信息全齐了才开始想。把未定项留清楚，后续拿到信息时也更容易知道该改哪一部分。
:::

依据前提是否已经确认，选择这一轮最有用的工作。

::play{#start-with-the-constraints-weigh}

## 什么时候该反过来

受众和形式已经确定、场地或平台也有真实确认时，就可以开始细化任务与负责人。不要每一轮都重问已经核实的条件，却迟迟不做下一步。

:::detail[怎样避免把常识当成这次的确认？]
“社区通常有活动室”不是你这次已经取得场地的证明；“大家应该都能上网”也不是参与者确实能使用某个平台的确认。可以在条件旁记录依据，例如负责人的明确回复、场地的规则或参与者需求。没有依据的部分继续写待确认。NASA指南提示要检查权限、容量与可访问性，但并未替你的具体场地批准这些条件。用实际信息填任务单，才把通用方法落到这次事情上。
:::

:::detail[条件后来变化，旧计划要全部扔掉吗？]
先看哪个任务依赖变化的条件。现场改线上，平台进入方式和参与说明需要重做；某些已经选好的公开月球资料仍可能保留。把条件与任务的连接写清楚，能帮助你局部修改，而不是每次从头要求一份新长文。新的计划仍需重新检查受影响的部分，不能只改标题就说安排已经更新。你要知道变了什么、保留什么，以及哪一项需要重新获得真实确认。
:::

## 自检

原计划为现场，后来改成线上。你会先标出哪些任务需要重新确认，而不是只替换计划标题？

## 一句话

**先确认会改变方案的条件，再细化时间与任务。**

en.title: List a Hundred Ideas First, or Ask Where It Will Be Held First?
en.content:
# List a Hundred Ideas First, or Ask Where It Will Be Held First?

## An Event Hosting Guide Starts by Asking Who You Plan to Invite

[NASA's Observe the Moon Night host guide](https://science.nasa.gov/moon/observe-the-moon-night/how-to-host/) provides a real-world reference for preparing a Moon observation event. You plan to use it to make a task list, but you have not yet decided on the format of the event.

You have not hosted an event or booked a venue, and your very first request right now is just: "Help me plan a great Observe the Moon Night."

## Predict first
Before asking for a detailed schedule, what conditions would you provide first that would alter the whole plan?

Write down your judgment first before looking at the answer below.

## Answer
State the audience, event format, available resources, and the venue or platform that still needs confirmation first. A polished schedule cannot decide these prerequisites for you, nor can it treat unconfirmed conditions as already arranged.

## Name the Conditions First, Then Add Details to the Plan

You can request: "First list the conditions that must be confirmed based on the guide, without filling in the attendance numbers, location, or lead organizers that I haven't provided yet; once these are clear, arrange the sequence of tasks."

Here, the AI helps you organize the questions, rather than inventing an already-approved event out of thin air.

:::detail[Does not having a confirmed headcount mean you cannot start at all?]
You can start with work that does not depend on an exact headcount, such as outlining possible formats and listing conditions to confirm along with relevant sources. Just do not write unconfirmed numbers into external commitments. A draft can have fields left to be filled in, and it can also explicitly compare what different preparations a small gathering versus an online presentation would require. You are advancing a bounded planning effort, not waiting until all information is fully in hand to start thinking. Leaving undecided items clearly marked also makes it easier to know which part to change when you get the information later.
:::

Choose the most useful work for this round based on whether prerequisites have been confirmed.

::play{#start-with-the-constraints-weigh}

## When to choose the other way

When the audience and format are already decided and the venue or platform has real confirmation, you can start detailing tasks and assignees. Do not keep re-asking about verified conditions in every round while holding off on the next step.

:::detail[How do you avoid mistaking common assumptions for actual confirmation this time?]
"The community center usually has an activity room" is not proof that you have secured the venue this time; "everyone should have internet access" is not confirmation that participants can actually use a particular platform. You can record evidence next to conditions, such as a clear response from the lead organizer, venue rules, or participant needs. For items without evidence, continue to mark them as pending confirmation. The NASA guide reminds you to check permits, capacity, and accessibility, but it does not approve these conditions for your specific venue. Filling the task list with real information is what applies the general method to this specific event.
:::

:::detail[If conditions change later, should the old plan be thrown out entirely?]
First look at which tasks depend on the changed conditions. If an in-person event moves online, the platform access method and participation instructions need to be redone; some publicly available lunar resources already selected may still be kept. Clearly mapping the connection between conditions and tasks helps you make targeted edits rather than asking for a brand-new long document from scratch every time. The new plan still requires rechecking the affected parts; you cannot just change the title and claim the schedule has been updated. You need to know what changed, what was kept, and which items need to be genuinely reconfirmed.
:::

## Check yourself
The original plan was in-person, but was later switched to online. Which tasks would you mark first as needing reconfirmation, instead of just swapping the plan's title?

## In one sentence
**Confirm the conditions that change the plan first, then detail the timeline and tasks.**

lessons.title: 为什么有些事情不能同时开始？
lessons.content:
# 为什么有些事情不能同时开始？

## 名单排出来了，但哪一步必须先发生？

[NASA主办指南](https://science.nasa.gov/moon/observe-the-moon-night/how-to-host/)让组织者先考虑受众与场地、检查当地观月条件，再推广已经安排好的活动。

你准备整理三个任务：确定参加方式、检查场地或平台是否适用、写出参加说明。它们可以都放进列表，却不适合不看前提就同时宣布完成。

## 先猜一下

哪些任务要先得到前一步的结果，后面的文字才有真实依据？

先写下你的判断，再往下看答案。

## 答案

先确定活动形式与参加需求，再检查相应场地或平台；参加说明应使用已经确认的结果。先后关系来自任务需要什么输入，不只是列表编号。

## 把“先做什么”改成“后一步需要什么”

写参加说明需要可靠的进入方式；核对进入方式，需要先知道使用现场地点还是线上平台。把这条关系接起来，就看得出哪一项尚未完成会影响后面。

请你在下面接好这条最小任务链。它根据真实指南中的准备关系设计，不是已经替任何人办妥了活动。

:::detail[任务链是不是把所有工作都排成一条长队？]
不是。有些任务不依赖同一项结果，可以分别准备。例如在条件尚未最终确定时，整理公开月球资料与列出待确认问题可以推进；只是不能把它们准备好了当成场地已确认。这里用三项任务练最基本的依赖关系，真正的计划可以有分支。先识别哪些步骤确实需要前一步的输出，再决定能否并行，而不是为了画一条整齐的箭头就让所有人等待同一个动作。
:::

:::detail[已经写出邀请草稿，是不是破坏了先后顺序？]
留出空位的草稿可以提前写，但对外使用前必须填入已经核实的条件。草稿完成与发布可用是两种不同状态。你可以标明参加方式待确认，后面再根据真实结果更新；不能把草稿里的暂定地点当成场地获准。把每项任务的结束条件写清楚，就不会因“文字已经有了”而误以为它依赖的现实动作也完成了。这里要保护的是交付状态，不是禁止提前思考。
:::

:::detail[前一步变了，怎样知道该重看后面哪一项？]
沿着依赖关系检查。现场改成线上，场地检查不再回答平台是否可进入；依赖它的参加说明也应更新。没有依赖这项变化的资料整理可能保留。你可以让AI根据任务链列出受影响项，但仍要实际核对完成状态与相关材料。图上的箭头是一份解释工具，不是自动执行器；它帮助你发现漏改的可能位置，不替你完成平台测试或通知参与者。
:::

把三项任务接成一条能解释输入从哪里来的链，再运行观察路径。

::play{#order-the-dependencies-connect}

## 自检

中间的平台进入方式发生变化。哪一项已写好的文字需要跟着复查，哪一项公开资料整理未必需要重做？

## 一句话

**前后顺序来自输入与依赖，不是任务列表的漂亮编号。**

en.title: Why Can't Some Things Start at the Same Time?
en.content:
# Why Can't Some Things Start at the Same Time?

## The list is made, but which step must happen first?

The [NASA host guide](https://science.nasa.gov/moon/observe-the-moon-night/how-to-host/) asks organizers to first consider their audience and venue and check local moon-viewing conditions before promoting an already-scheduled event.

You are preparing to organize three tasks: determine participation format, check whether the venue or platform is suitable, and write participation instructions. They can all go into a list, but it is not appropriate to declare them all complete at the same time without looking at prerequisites.

## Predict first
Which tasks must first obtain the results of an earlier step so that subsequent text has a real basis?

Write down your judgment first, then scroll down to see the answer.

## Answer
First determine the event format and participation requirements, then check the corresponding venue or platform; participation instructions should use already-confirmed results. Sequence comes from what inputs a task needs, not just list numbers.

## Change "what to do first" to "what the next step needs"

Writing participation instructions requires a reliable way to enter; verifying the entry method requires knowing first whether an in-person venue or an online platform is being used. Connecting this relationship makes it clear which unfinished item will affect subsequent steps.

Please connect this minimal task chain below. It is designed around the preparation relationships in real guidelines, rather than having already settled an event for anyone.

:::detail[Does a task chain line up all work into a single long queue?]
No. Some tasks do not depend on the same outcome and can be prepared separately. For example, while conditions are not yet finalized, compiling public lunar materials and listing open questions can move forward; you just cannot treat their readiness as confirmation of the venue. Here, three tasks are used to practice the most basic dependency relationship; real plans can have branches. First identify which steps genuinely require the output of a prior step, then decide whether they can run in parallel, rather than making everyone wait on the same single action just to draw a neat arrow.
:::

:::detail[Does having written an invitation draft break the sequence?]
Drafts with placeholders can be written ahead of time, but before being used externally, verified conditions must be filled in. Being done with a draft and being ready for release are two different states. You can mark the participation method as pending confirmation and update it later based on real outcomes; you cannot treat a tentative location in a draft as venue approval. Stating the exit criteria for each task clearly prevents assuming the underlying real-world action is complete just because "the text already exists." What is being protected here is delivery status, not a ban on thinking ahead.
:::

:::detail[When an earlier step changes, how do you know which later item to revisit?]
Trace along the dependency chain. If in-person changes to online, the venue check no longer answers whether the platform is accessible; the participation instructions relying on it should also be updated. Compiling materials that do not depend on this change may be retained. You can have AI list affected items based on the task chain, but you still need to verify actual completion status and related materials yourself. The arrows on a diagram are an explanatory tool, not an automatic executor; they help you spot potential places where updates were missed, without running platform tests or notifying attendees for you.
:::

Connect the three tasks into a chain that explains where inputs come from, then run it to observe the path.

::play{#order-the-dependencies-connect}

## Check yourself
The platform access method in the middle changes. Which drafted text needs to be reviewed alongside it, and which compilation of public materials may not need to be redone?

## In one sentence
**Sequence comes from inputs and dependencies, not tidy numbering on a task list.**

lessons.title: 清单打满勾，就一定准备够了吗？
lessons.content:
# 清单打满勾，就一定准备够了吗？

## 清单已经全打勾，事情就一定没问题吗？

[美国国家公园管理局的行程规划指南](https://www.nps.gov/subjects/healthandsafety/trip-planning-guide.htm)说明自己的日间与过夜出行范围，并指出多日野外行程还需要额外准备。它的[必备物品页](https://www.nps.gov/articles/10essentials.htm)也提醒按具体活动增加所需装备。

这里不推荐任何实际路线，只借这两份真实材料检查一种常见说法：“清单全做完，就已经保证适合所有活动。”

## 先猜一下

一份有用的准备清单，与对某次活动已经适合的确认，中间还差什么？

先写下你的判断，再往下看答案。

## 答案

还要核对清单的适用范围，以及这次活动的具体条件。完成通用准备，不会自动证明范围之外的事情也已经确认。

## 清单告诉你检查什么，不替现实条件作证

把每项分成“已经列出”“已经核对”“仍待确认”，比只放一个勾更清楚。你有一个检查位置，不等于已经取得那个位置的结果。

同样，[NASA观月夜指南](https://science.nasa.gov/moon/observe-the-moon-night/how-to-host/)列出场地权限、可访问性与阴雨预案，也没有替你的场地批准任何安排。

:::detail[为什么有清单仍然值得做，而不是干脆不做？]
清单能帮助你不漏掉常见准备项目，也让不同人共享要检查的内容。它的局限是不能自动覆盖所有情境、不能保证执行质量，更不能让未来条件不变化。你可以把它当成组织工作的起点，配上具体对象、核对方式与负责人。这样的清单比只写“都准备好了”更容易交接。承认它不是保证，并不会削弱它的价值，反而让你知道什么时候需要补充而不是机械照抄。
:::

比较两种清单用法：机械把完成当保证，或核对范围后再解释完成状态。这里只比较明确的使用规则。

::play{#a-list-is-not-a-guarantee-contrast}

## 相同文字，也可能对应不同适用范围

一项任务恰好落在指南说明的范围里，可以据此继续检查；超出范围时，就另找相应信息。不是因为来源官方，就把它说成回答了所有问题。

:::detail[怎样向AI提要求，避免把清单写成保证？]
可以说：“按这份材料列出准备项，并保留适用范围；不要把尚未核实的状态填成完成，也不要保证活动结果。”随后查看它是否在结尾又加了“这样就万无一失”之类的话。删掉这种话不是为了让文章显得谨慎，而是恢复材料实际支持的程度。真正的完成状态来自记录与检查，不能由写作模型替尚未发生的动作宣布成功。
:::

:::detail[复制上一场活动的清单时，先改什么？]
先核对这一次的活动形式、地点、参加者需求与条件变化，再看哪些检查仍然适用。一个上次已确认的场地，不代表这次相同时间也获准使用；一个平台上次可用，也可能需要重新测试。你可以保留清单的结构与常见问题，但完成状态要属于这一次实际任务。把方法和结果分开复用，就能减少重复劳动，同时不把历史勾选记录当成新事实。你可以在原来的勾选旁另写本次的确认状态，让两个时点同时看得见。这样接手者能知道哪条是历史经验，哪条是今天实际取得的结果，不必猜测整张表是否更新过。
:::

## 自检

你把上次活动的清单复用到新地点。为什么可以沿用检查问题，却不能连完成勾选一起照搬？

## 一句话

**清单组织准备，真实条件决定哪些事情已经确认。**

en.title: Does Checking Every Box Mean You Are Definitely Prepared?
en.content:
# Does Checking Every Box Mean You Are Definitely Prepared?

## If every box on a checklist is checked, is everything definitely fine?

The [National Park Service's trip planning guide](https://www.nps.gov/subjects/healthandsafety/trip-planning-guide.htm) outlines its scope for day and overnight outings, noting that multi-day backcountry trips require additional preparation. Its [essentials page](https://www.nps.gov/articles/10essentials.htm) also reminds you to add necessary gear based on the specific activity.

No actual routes are recommended here; these two real sources are used solely to examine a common claim: "Once the checklist is completely done, it is already guaranteed to be suitable for all activities."

## Predict first
What is still missing between a useful preparation checklist and the confirmation that you are ready for a specific activity?

Write down your judgment first, then read on for the answer.

## Answer
You still need to check the checklist's scope of application and the specific conditions of this activity. Completing general preparation does not automatically prove that things outside its scope have also been confirmed.

## A checklist tells you what to check, not testify to real-world conditions

Dividing each item into "already listed," "already checked," and "still pending confirmation" is clearer than just leaving a single checkmark. Having a place to check does not mean you have already obtained the result for that place.

Similarly, [NASA's Observe the Moon Night guide](https://science.nasa.gov/moon/observe-the-moon-night/how-to-host/) lists venue permissions, accessibility, and backup plans for cloudy or rainy weather, but it does not approve any arrangements for your venue.

:::detail[Why is having a checklist still worth doing instead of skipping it altogether?]
A checklist helps you avoid missing common preparation items, and it allows different people to share what needs to be checked. Its limitation is that it cannot automatically cover all situations, cannot guarantee execution quality, and certainly cannot prevent future conditions from changing. You can treat it as a starting point for organizing work, pairing it with specific targets, verification methods, and responsible owners. Such a checklist is much easier to hand off than simply writing "everything is ready." Acknowledging that it is not a guarantee does not diminish its value; rather, it lets you know when you need to add supplements instead of copying it mechanically.
:::

Compare two ways of using checklists: mechanically treating completion as a guarantee, or interpreting completion status only after checking the scope. Only explicit usage rules are compared here.

::play{#a-list-is-not-a-guarantee-contrast}

## Identical text may still apply to different scopes

If a task happens to fall within the scope explained by the guide, you can continue checking based on it; when it falls outside that scope, look for corresponding information elsewhere. Just because a source is official does not mean it answers every question.

:::detail[How should you prompt an AI to avoid turning a checklist into a guarantee?]
You can say: "List the preparation items based on this material and preserve the applicable scope; do not mark unverified statuses as completed, and do not guarantee the outcome of the event." Then check whether it added something like "this guarantees nothing can go wrong" at the end. Deleting such statements is not about making the writing seem cautious, but about restoring what the material actually supports. A true completion status comes from records and checks; a writing model cannot declare success for actions that have not yet occurred.
:::

:::detail[When copying a checklist from a previous event, what should you change first?]
First check this event's format, venue, participant needs, and changing conditions, then see which checks are still applicable. A venue confirmed last time does not mean it is approved for use at the same time this time; a platform that was usable last time may still need to be retested. You can keep the checklist's structure and common questions, but the completion status must belong to this specific task. Reusing methods and results separately reduces redundant work without mistaking past checkmarks for new facts. You can write this event's confirmation status next to the original checkmarks so that both points in time are visible at once. This way, whoever takes over knows which item is past experience and which is a result actually obtained today, without having to guess whether the whole sheet was updated.
:::

## Check yourself
You reuse a checklist from a previous event at a new location. Why can you carry over the checklist questions, but not copy over the completion checkmarks as well?

## In one sentence
**A checklist organizes preparation; real conditions determine what has been confirmed.**

lessons.title: 天气不配合，这个计划就只能取消吗？
lessons.content:
# 天气不配合，这个计划就只能取消吗？

## 看不到月亮时，还能完成哪一个目标？

[NASA的观月夜主办指南](https://science.nasa.gov/moon/observe-the-moon-night/how-to-host/)询问组织者遇到阴雨怎么办，并提供通过图像、可视化和线上资源了解月球的替代路径。

你在做一份筹备任务单，目标是帮助参与者认识月面，而不是承诺当晚每个人都能直接看到真实月亮。现在要为直接观察无法进行的情况保留一条路径。

## 先猜一下

选择备用方案时，你会先保留原计划里的什么，而不是只想找个节目填满时间？

先写下你的判断，再往下看答案。

## 答案

先保留参与者要获得的具体收获，再选择在新条件下能完成它的方式。若要学习月面特征，真实图像与资料可以成为替代；不能因此把间接查看说成已经现场观测。

## 换做法，不偷换学习目标

你可以在任务单上写两条路径：条件合适时直接观察；无法观察时，用来源清楚的图像完成识别与讨论。两条路径都说明具体要做的事与所需材料。

这是一份依据指南的备用安排，不是本地天气预报。真正举办前还需核对当时条件。

:::detail[为什么不能把任何有趣视频都当备用？]
先看它是否帮助参与者完成原来的目标。一个与月面无关的热门视频可能吸引注意，却没有继续这次学习。你可以改变媒介、缩小范围或调整活动长度，但最好说清保留的是哪一项收获。如果目标本来就是共同欣赏月球文化作品，那么合适的文化材料也可能符合；重点不是所有备用都必须讲同一张图，而是别在条件变化后忘记原来想让参与者得到什么。
:::

同一种替代方式，在不同学习目标下是否足够？

::play{#plan-for-the-clouds-weigh}

## 什么时候该反过来

目标若是练习亲自操作某种观测设备，单看图像不能声称完成了那项实操。可以改期、缩成介绍，或明确记录尚未完成的部分，而不是把备用活动算作同一种经历。

:::detail[备用计划怎样写得让接手的人真能使用？]
写清何时需要切换、替代活动是什么、材料从哪里来、谁来确认与通知。只写“天气不好就有备用”没有交代实际动作，也让参与者不知道怎样得到更新。对本课任务单，可以先把具体日期、联系人与确认方式留为需要真实填入的项目，不随便编人名。你正在设计一个可接手的流程；等实际条件齐全，再把它变成某次活动的正式安排。
:::

:::detail[备用方案一定要与原方案一样丰富吗？]
不一定。可以保留一个小而明确的核心活动，减少对更多资源的依赖。例如只完成一张月面图的观察与说明，也比声称准备了一整套尚不存在的线上活动更容易核查。写出这条方案放弃了什么、保留了什么，让人能够决定是否接受。计划的价值是把选择与后果说清，不是保证无论发生什么都能交付同一种体验。先让替代活动真实可用，再决定是否扩充。
:::

## 自检

一个备用活动很好玩，却不再帮助完成原来选定的目标。怎样缩小或调整它，才能说明保留了什么？

## 一句话

**备用方案先保住明确目标，做不到的部分也如实留下。**

en.title: If the Weather Doesn't Cooperate, Must the Plan Be Canceled?
en.content:
# If the Weather Doesn't Cooperate, Must the Plan Be Canceled?

## When the Moon Isn't Visible, Which Goal Can Still Be Accomplished?

[NASA's Observe the Moon Night Host Guide](https://science.nasa.gov/moon/observe-the-moon-night/how-to-host/) asks organizers what to do in case of cloudy or rainy weather, and provides alternative paths to learn about the Moon through images, visualizations, and online resources.

You are preparing an event planning task sheet. The goal is to help participants learn about lunar surface features, not to promise that everyone will directly see the actual Moon that night. Now you need to reserve a path for when direct observation is not possible.

## Predict first
When choosing a backup plan, what from the original plan would you preserve first, rather than simply looking for an activity to fill the time?

Write down your judgment first, then read on for the answer.

## Answer
First preserve the specific takeaways participants are supposed to gain, and then select a way to achieve them under the new conditions. If the goal is to learn lunar surface features, real images and reference materials can serve as substitutes; you cannot, however, claim that indirect viewing is the same as having observed the Moon on site.

## Change the Approach, Don't Switch the Learning Goal

You can write two paths on the task sheet: direct observation when conditions are suitable; and when observation is impossible, using well-sourced images to complete identification and discussion. Both paths should explain the specific actions to take and the materials required.

This is a backup arrangement based on the guide, not a local weather forecast. Before actually hosting the event, you still need to check the conditions at that time.

:::detail[Why can't just any entertaining video serve as a backup?]
First look at whether it helps participants achieve the original goal. A trending video unrelated to the lunar surface might draw attention, but it does not continue the planned learning. You can change the medium, narrow the scope, or adjust the activity's length, but it is best to state clearly which takeaway is being preserved. If the goal was originally to appreciate lunar cultural works together, then appropriate cultural materials might also fit. The point is not that every backup must use the exact same image, but rather not forgetting what participants were supposed to gain once conditions change.
:::

Is the same substitute method sufficient under different learning goals?

::play{#plan-for-the-clouds-weigh}

## When to choose the other way

If the goal is to practice operating observation equipment in person, merely viewing images cannot count as having completed that hands-on practice. You can reschedule, scale it down to an introduction, or explicitly record the unfinished parts, rather than treating the backup activity as the same experience.

:::detail[How can a backup plan be written so that someone taking over can actually use it?]
State clearly when to switch, what the alternative activity is, where materials come from, and who confirms and notifies people. Merely writing "there is a backup if the weather is bad" fails to explain the actual actions and leaves participants unsure how they will receive updates. For this lesson's task sheet, you can leave specific dates, contacts, and confirmation methods as fields to be filled in with real information later, rather than making up names. You are designing a handover-ready workflow; once actual conditions are in place, you can turn it into a formal schedule for a specific event.
:::

:::detail[Does a backup plan have to be as elaborate as the original plan?]
Not necessarily. You can keep a small, clear core activity to reduce dependence on additional resources. For instance, completing the observation and explanation of just a single lunar surface image is much easier to verify than claiming to have prepared an entire suite of non-existent online activities. Spell out what this plan gives up and what it preserves, allowing people to decide whether to accept it. The value of planning lies in making choices and consequences clear, not in guaranteeing that the exact same experience will be delivered no matter what happens. Make the substitute activity genuinely usable first before deciding whether to expand it.
:::

## Check yourself
A backup activity is very entertaining, but it no longer helps fulfill the originally chosen goal. How would you narrow or adjust it so that what has been preserved is clear?

## In one sentence
**A backup plan first secures a clear goal, while truthfully recording what cannot be done.**

lessons.title: 写着“准备好了”，到底谁确认过？
lessons.content:
# 写着“准备好了”，到底谁确认过？

## 写上负责人，等于有人答应了吗？

[NASA观月夜指南](https://science.nasa.gov/moon/observe-the-moon-night/how-to-host/)把寻找协助者、布置与活动后的清理都列入考虑。你让AI据此生成任务清单，里面出现了“联系场地”“整理材料”“完成收尾”。

这些都是可讨论的任务，但你还没有安排任何真人接手。

## 先猜一下

要让清单变成可交接的工作，每一项还需要说明什么？

先写下你的判断，再往下看答案。

## 答案

说明具体动作、需要的输入、谁来负责以及怎样确认完成。负责人的名字只有在本人或相应流程确认后，才能被当成真实安排。

## 一项任务，让接手者知道拿什么、交什么

可以把“整理材料”改成“按选定主题收集来源清楚的月面图，记录原始入口与使用说明，交给确认过的编辑人复查”。未知的人与时间先保留待定。

你请AI写的是工作说明，不是替别人接受任务。把草拟分工与已确认分工分开。

:::detail[为什么只写“大家一起做”不容易接手？]
遇到遗漏时，很难知道谁在等谁、哪一步还没人处理。给动作一个明确负责人，不是要把合作搞复杂，而是让一项结果有可追问的落点。小任务也可以由同一个人承担多项，只要知道各项需要的输入与结束条件。你作为个人学习者可以先写“由我完成”，再记录实际做到了哪里；没有发生的联系、许可或测试，仍然不能因为负责人是自己就直接打勾。
:::

:::detail[怎样区分任务已提出与任务已接受？]
一份自动生成的名单只说明建议谁可能负责，不代表对方已收到或同意。可以给状态留清楚的文字，例如待邀请、已确认负责、已交付待检查。接手时先看状态，不要把所有名字都当成已经承诺的资源。对本课练习，不需要真的联系陌生人；你只要能够在任务单中区分这种状态，就已经避免了一种容易在AI生成计划里出现的误会。
:::

:::detail[完成标准必须写得很长吗？]
写到足以判断当前动作是否结束即可。例如整理图片需要提供选中的文件或入口、出处和使用说明；它不必同时承担整个活动是否成功的评价。标准太宽会让一个小任务永远结束不了，太空则容易让“我做了”没有可以查看的结果。你可以从准备交给下一步的东西倒推：下一位需要看到什么，才有条件继续工作？把这个结果写出来，通常比抽象地要求“认真完成”更清楚。
:::

把任务清单中的记录按真实状态分开。卡片是筹备记录练习，不代表已有人接受本课安排。

::play{#who-does-what-sort}

## 自检

负责人说已完成，但没有提供下一步需要的文件或入口。你会补问哪项具体结果，而不是只再问一遍完成没有？

## 一句话

**分工写清动作与结果，接受任务和完成任务分别确认。**

en.title: Marked "Ready"—Who Actually Confirmed It?
en.content:
# Marked "Ready"—Who Actually Confirmed It?

## Does Listing an Assignee Mean Someone Agreed?

The [NASA Observe the Moon Night Guide](https://science.nasa.gov/moon/observe-the-moon-night/how-to-host/) takes finding helpers, setup, and post-event cleanup into account. You ask an AI to generate a task list based on it, and items like "contact the venue," "organize materials," and "wrap things up" appear.

These are all workable tasks, but you have not yet arranged for any real person to take them on.

## Predict first
To turn this checklist into handoff-ready work, what else must each item specify?

Write down your thoughts first, then scroll down to see the answer.

## Answer
Specify the concrete action, the required inputs, who is responsible, and how completion is confirmed. An assignee's name can only be treated as a real commitment after that person or the relevant process has confirmed it.

## A Task: Let the Assignee Know What to Take and What to Deliver

You can change "organize materials" to "collect lunar surface images with clear sources based on the chosen topic, record original access points and usage instructions, and hand them over to a confirmed editor for review." Keep unknown people and dates marked as pending for now.

What you asked the AI to write is a work breakdown, not an agreement to accept tasks on someone else's behalf. Keep drafted assignments separate from confirmed assignments.

:::detail[Why is it hard to hand off when a task just says "everyone work together"?]
When something falls through the cracks, it is hard to tell who is waiting on whom or which step remains unaddressed. Giving an action a clear owner is not about making collaboration complicated; it gives an outcome a clear point of accountability. One person can also take on multiple small tasks, as long as the inputs and completion criteria for each are known. As an individual learner, you can start by writing "completed by me" and then log how far you actually got; outreach, permissions, or testing that never happened still cannot be checked off just because you are the owner yourself.
:::

:::detail[How do you distinguish a proposed task from an accepted task?]
An automatically generated list only suggests who might be responsible; it does not mean that person has received the request or agreed. You can use clear wording for statuses, such as Pending Invitation, Confirmed Owner, or Delivered Pending Review. When taking over a project, check the status first, rather than treating every name as a committed resource. For this lesson's exercise, you do not need to contact real strangers; simply being able to distinguish these statuses on a task sheet avoids a common misunderstanding in AI-generated plans.
:::

:::detail[Must completion criteria be written in great detail?]
Writing enough to determine whether the current action is finished is sufficient. For instance, organizing images requires providing the selected files or links, sources, and usage notes; it does not also need to evaluate whether the entire event succeeded. Criteria that are too broad make a small task drag on forever, while criteria that are too vague make "I did it" lack any verifiable outcome. You can work backward from what you prepare to hand off to the next step: what does the next person need to see before they can continue working? Writing down that deliverable is usually much clearer than an abstract demand to "complete it carefully."
:::

Separate the entries on the task list by their actual status. The cards are an exercise in prep logging and do not mean anyone has accepted arrangements for this lesson.

::play{#who-does-what-sort}

## Check yourself
The assignee says they are done, but has not provided the files or access links needed for the next step. What specific deliverable would you ask for, rather than just asking again whether it is finished?

## In one sentence
**Define assignments clearly with actions and outcomes, and confirm task acceptance and task completion separately.**

lessons.title: 别人能按这份计划接着做吗？
lessons.content:
# 别人能按这份计划接着做吗？

## 最后留下的，不只是一张漂亮时间表

你已经依据[NASA观月夜指南](https://science.nasa.gov/moon/observe-the-moon-night/how-to-host/)区分受众与条件、任务依赖、备用安排和负责状态。现在把它们收拢成一份自己的筹备任务单。

你不需要真的去办活动，而要让接手的人知道已经确定什么、下一步查什么，以及条件变化时怎样调整。

## 先猜一下

这份任务单交给另一个人以后，他应当能从里面找到哪几种信息？

先写下你的判断，再往下看答案。

## 答案

能找到目标与条件、下一项动作、负责人或待确认项，以及完成依据和备用分支。计划能被检查和修正，比看起来安排得非常满更重要。

## 自己做一页，再沿着它走一遍

写四块：目标与前提、任务及依赖、未确认事项、备用安排。至少给一项任务写出实际输入与交付物，再标明是否已经发生。

可以请AI按这四块检查你的草稿是否有遗漏，但是否真正得到许可、收到确认或完成测试，仍要看实际记录。

:::detail[为什么不在最后提供一份直接照抄的完整计划？]
你现在练的是把真实指南用到一份范围明确的成品里，而不是收藏第六份模板。可以参考前面的字段，但由你决定哪些适合当前任务，哪些仍然需要补查。把未定项写出来也是合格的筹备成果，不代表你必须在课程里安排真实场地或联系参与者。一个诚实的候选任务单，比一份虚构所有条件都满足的“完成计划”更容易继续使用。最后要检查的是它是否能被接手，而不是它有没有把所有格子填满。
:::

下面是一份根据真实指南编写的教学筹备记录，不代表实际有人承诺或活动已经安排。综合查看目标、依赖、负责人和备用状态，再决定下一步。

::play{#make-a-plan-you-can-review-weigh}

## 什么时候该反过来

计划中的关键前提已经变化时，先修受影响的任务与承诺，不急着美化版面。边界稳定、内容能接手以后，再让文字更短、层级更清楚。

:::detail[怎样检查另一人是否真的能接着做？]
自己扮演第一次看到这页的人，只按页面去找：下一步是什么、需要谁确认、到哪里查资料、怎样判断完成。缺一个入口或状态，就把它补成具体问题，而不是靠你口头解释过去。以后有实际协作者时，可以让对方做同样的试读，记录真实卡点；本次没有真人参与，就不要把自查写成已通过用户验收。你可以把两类证据分开保留，逐步改进任务单。
:::

:::detail[活动结束以后，这份计划还剩什么价值？]
指南也安排了反馈与回顾。你可以把原计划与实际发生的步骤对照，记录哪一项输入不充分、哪个备用方案被用到、哪些任务需要下次改变。没有实际举办时，就只保留筹备层面的检查，不编造参与者意见。这样的记录让下一次复用的是有效方法与具体教训，而不是一份处处顺利的漂亮总结。计划与真实结果分开保存，才能看见差异。
:::

## 自检

遮住你自己的补充说明，只看一页任务单。能否指出下一步、一个真实来源、一个未确认项，以及变化时要重看哪条依赖？

## 一句话

**能接手、能核对、能修正的计划，才不只是一份漂亮文本。**

en.title: Can Someone Else Take Over from This Plan?
en.content:
# Can Someone Else Take Over from This Plan?

## Leaving Behind More Than Just a Pretty Schedule

You have already used the [NASA Observe the Moon Night guide](https://science.nasa.gov/moon/observe-the-moon-night/how-to-host/) to distinguish audiences and conditions, task dependencies, backup arrangements, and ownership statuses. Now bring them together into your own preparation task list.

You do not need to actually run the event; instead, make sure whoever takes over knows what has been confirmed, what to check next, and how to adapt when conditions change.

## Predict first
Once this task list is handed to another person, what kinds of information should they be able to find in it?

Write down your judgment first before looking at the answer below.

## Answer
They should be able to find goals and conditions, next actions, owners or items pending confirmation, as well as completion criteria and backup branches. Being able to inspect and revise a plan is more important than making it look packed.

## Build a One-Page Plan, Then Walk Through It

Write four sections: goals and prerequisites, tasks and dependencies, unconfirmed items, and backup arrangements. For at least one task, write out actual inputs and deliverables, and indicate whether it has already occurred.

You can ask an AI to check your draft across these four sections for any omissions, but whether you have actually secured permission, received confirmation, or finished testing still depends on real records.

:::detail[Why not provide a complete plan at the end to copy directly?]
What you are practicing now is applying a real guide to a well-scoped deliverable, rather than collecting a sixth template. You can refer to the earlier fields, but it is up to you to decide which ones fit the current task and which ones still require further checking. Writing down undecided items is also a valid preparation outcome; it does not mean you must book a real venue or contact participants during this course. An honest candidate task list is much easier to keep using than a "completed plan" that fabricates satisfying every condition. What you ultimately need to check is whether someone else can take it over, not whether every box is filled.
:::

Below is an instructional prep record based on a real guide; it does not mean anyone has actually made commitments or that an event has been scheduled. Review the goals, dependencies, owners, and backup statuses as a whole before deciding on the next step.

::play{#make-a-plan-you-can-review-weigh}

## When to choose the other way

When key prerequisites in the plan have changed, fix the affected tasks and commitments first instead of rushing to polish the layout. Once boundaries are stable and the content can be handed off, make the wording more concise and the hierarchy clearer.

:::detail[How do you check whether someone else can truly take over?]
Role-play as someone seeing this page for the first time, and search solely based on what is on the page: what the next step is, who needs to confirm, where to find reference materials, and how to tell when something is done. If an entry point or status is missing, flesh it out into a specific question rather than glossing over it with a verbal explanation. When you have real collaborators in the future, you can have them do the same trial run and note actual sticking points; since no real people are participating this time, do not record a self-check as having passed user acceptance. You can keep these two types of evidence separate and improve the task list step by step.
:::

:::detail[Once the event is over, what value is left in this plan?]
The guide also includes feedback and a retrospective. You can compare the original plan against the steps that actually happened, noting which input was insufficient, which backup option was used, and which tasks need to change next time. When you haven't actually hosted the event, keep only the checks at the prep level and do not fabricate participant feedback. A record like this ensures that what you reuse next time is effective methods and concrete lessons, rather than a pretty summary where everything went smoothly. Keep the plan and the real outcomes separate so you can see the differences.
:::

## Check yourself
Cover your own supplemental notes and look only at the one-page task list. Can you point out the next step, a real source, an unconfirmed item, and which dependency to recheck if conditions change?

## In one sentence
**A plan that can be taken over, checked, and revised is more than just pretty text.**
